candidates.title: Cloud puffs: fog once per sprite, early exit, and an incremental sort
candidates.plainSummary: About 1,000 cloud puffs are flat sprites. Every pixel of every sprite redoes fog maths whose answer is the same across the whole sprite. Meanwhile, on every moving frame, the CPU re-sorts all of the puffs from scratch and creates about 1,000 throwaway array views. Doing the fog once per sprite, skipping invisible rim pixels, and updating the previous sort order gives the same picture for less work.

Per-tier counts for flames, spray, mist, petals, birds and motes; grass reach and density by tier.

gaps: No frame times on weak hardware. The live run used an RTX 5080 with forced tiers, so it gave draw and triangle counts, not milliseconds. Every ms figure above is an estimate from op counts, code structure or the repo's own comments.

The GLB files are Git LFS pointers here, so I could not see how much of the screen each material covers, triangle sizes, or how many tree cards there are. That limits the size estimates for C1, C2, C9 and C13.
The compositor cost of the backdrop blurs (C6) is not profiled. A Chrome performance trace while flying would settle it.
KTX2 size and quality against today's WebP q82 is untested. One atlas trial is needed before C12.
I did not check whether three r186 sorts opaque objects front to back by default. That affects how much early depth rejection C1 gets.

The main-thread time of the grass build on phones was not measured (stats().areas[id].buildMs). That matters for C16, and for a possible worker-based grass build (left out, because measured per-frame grass CPU is only 0.05-0.16 ms).

Left out because they cost some quality, or the gain was unclear: anisotropy per tier (lowers the Low and Mid look), bloom prefilter at half resolution (could dim sparks on High), R11G11B10 main buffer (banding risk), half-resolution cloud overlay (halo risk), a fog lookup table, a baked sky environment and a range-weight texture (larger jobs with uncertain size; worth a second round), and holding fewer decoded music tracks on phones (memory only, about 38 MB).

verdicts.reason: Holds up. The cloud sea material is opaque: no transparent flag, and depth writes are on by default (materials.ts:1373-1376). That puts it in three's opaque list, where renderOrder -800 draws it before the whole world (scene.tsx:475). The moon disc and halo are transparent (materials.ts:1250-1251, 1333-1335), so they sit in the transparent list and the -900/-901 orders do not interact with the sea. The sky stays at 1000, after any value up to 999. The glsl.ts:476-479 note is about the order of cloud and haze maths inside the fog function, not draw order, so it is unaffected. Nothing opaque uses an unusual depth function except the sky (depthFunc appears only at scene.tsx:435). One caveat to measure: terrain that hangs below y=-60 (island roots, pillar bases going into the sea; meta cloudSea.y = -60) is rejected early today because the sea's depth is already written. After the move, that terrain gets shaded and then covered, which eats into the saving. Measure the world pass with the GPU timer at the gate and 2-3 other stops, the way the sky move was measured. It also helps the pond and mirror reflection passes, which draw the sea too.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Unmeasured. Probably a few percent up to about 12% of the world pass in views where islands cover the sea, less where terrain dips below y=-60. Near zero elsewhere. Measure before quoting ms.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None. Depth testing decides what shows, and the moon and sky orders are unaffected.

verdicts.reason: Sound idea with small errors. The fog inputs really are the same across each sprite: vF and vDist come from iCenter in the vertex shader (materials.ts:1828-1849). So haze depth, haze colour, cloud depth and 'toward' (materials.ts:1902-1907) can move to the vertex shader as varyings. The result is visually exact but not bit-exact, because interpolated varyings can differ in the last bits. The per-pixel saving is bigger than claimed. sectHazeDepth costs 4-6 exp (two haze spans plus mist), sectHazeColor has a pow, the two 1-exp mixes add 2 more, sectCloudDepth adds 2, and 'toward' is a pow: about 11 exp plus 2 pow per pixel, not 8 special-function ops in total. The mist sprites follow the same pattern (vDir/vDist per instance, materials.ts:1975-1976). The early-discard claim is wrong for Mid and High: the composer buffer is half-float (effects.ts:200), not 8-bit. Also, the two noise reads and the soft-depth read must run before alpha is known, so the discard only skips the lighting tail. Keep the threshold tiny or skip it. The CPU part is right. Uint32Array.sort with a JS comparator makes about 10k comparator calls for 1021 puffs (clouds.ts:63-78). packed.subarray allocates about 1021 view objects per moving frame (scene.tsx:655-657), roughly 60-100 KB of garbage. Re-sorting from the previous order with insertion sort (the list is nearly sorted) and copying the 13 floats by hand gives the same order. The 0.5 m re-sort distance should stay.
verdicts.correctedSaving: GPU: about 60-80 ALU ops plus about 13 exp/pow per puff pixel, so 0.3-1 ms on an integrated GPU in cloud banks is plausible. CPU: about 0.1-0.3 ms per moving frame on desktop and 0.5-1.5 ms on a weak phone, plus about 60-100 KB less garbage per moving frame.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None visible: vertex-computed fog equals the per-pixel result to rounding. Drop or tighten the early discard on Mid and High, because their buffers are half-float, so 'below 8-bit' does not apply there.

verdicts.reason: The reordering is valid, and the output is bit-identical: when shade or lit is exactly 0, the factor is exactly 1.0. An early return inside mainImage is fine in a merged EffectPass, because each effect's mainImage is its own function. The saving is overstated, though. The most expensive part is the 3-octave noise (12 hashes, roughly 180 ops), and it still has to run on every lit pixel. What gets skipped is the transmittance (about 9 exp in sectHazeDepth, sectCloudDepth and the final exp) on pixels under clear deck. With cover [0.5, 0.74] that is about half the area (post.ts cover). Everything after the luma test can also be skipped on the minority of pixels that are deep shade (luma under 0.02) or glows (luma over 2.2). The world-position unprojection is needed for the keep fade and the noise anyway. Net: roughly 15-30% of this pass's ALU, not 30-50%. This pass only exists while bloom is on (post.ts:29-35). A Mid device the ladder has already stepped below bloom no longer runs it, so the gain goes to devices that keep bloom, where it may stop them stepping down.
verdicts.correctedSaving: About 15-30% of the cloud-shadow pass. Roughly 0.1-0.4 ms on a weak integrated GPU at 1080p, near 0 on a discrete GPU. It applies only while bloom (and so this pass) is on.

verdicts.reason: Partly right, but the benefit is misdescribed. Pond: in flight the pose changes every frame, so nothing can be reused. Reuse only applies at rest. At rest the page already renders at an idle 30 fps, or 20 fps after 20 s with no input (scene.tsx:1728-1731, 1949-1953). So this saves GPU power and heat at the Mirror and gate stops, not frame time or smoothness. Devices that are short of time already skip the pond pass: it is off once the ladder reaches stand-ins (reflect/index.ts:132, !f.lean). The pond view already leaves out grass and draws the other areas as stand-ins (plan.ts:25). Its camera is also narrowed to the pond's screen rectangle (plan.ts narrowProjection), so '2.5M triangles' is a loose upper bound. Implementation catch: update() clears uHasReflect and tReflect every frame (index.ts:99-103), and uWaterTime only advances inside renderPond (index.ts:242). Reuse must keep feeding both, or the ripples freeze. Cube: it is already one face per frame (plan.ts ProbeSchedule), and its content comes from the mirror's fixed capture point, not the main camera. The better fix is to skip timed refreshes while the camera moves (keep the refresh on signature changes) and keep 6 s at rest, where an extra face at a 30 fps idle rate is not seen. Do not stretch High's refresh to 15-20 s. The bronze face reflects strongly (f0 0.8), so drifting clouds would jump three times as far at each refresh, and that pop would show on High. The 'double-cost' frames were not measured: check with window.__sectReflect and the span timer.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Pond: GPU power and heat only, while resting near the pond (2 of 3 idle renders skip one narrowed scene pass). No frame-time gain in flight. Cube: removes one burst of 6 heavier frames per in-flight pass near the mirror. Measure the per-face cost before claiming 'double'.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: Pond at rest: reflected slow content (sky clouds, cranes, the mirror's breathing glow) updates at about 7-10 Hz under ripples, likely invisible, but check on High at the Heart-Mirror stop. Cube: none if timed refreshes are deferred only while the camera moves. A visible pop on High if the refresh interval is lengthened.

verdicts.reason: The main idea is sound. The stack is branch-free on purpose (detail.ts:780-784), and the distance fades only multiply the result (detail.ts:798-813, 835-841). A distance branch is spatially coherent, and textureGrad with derivatives taken outside the branch keeps the mip choice correct, as paving already does (detail.ts:692-693). It is not already done. Corrections: (1) Only some layers die far away. Rock detail is gone past 150 m (6 reads) and ground detail past 140 m (2). Clumps are gone past 260 m (2) and sheen past 320 m (1). The far-rock layer (sectRockFar, 1-2 reads, active from 50 to 700 m), the rock streaks (1 read) and the ground tint (never faded) must still run far away, so far rock saves about 6 reads, plus 2 more only for mossy rock past 260 m. (2) The waterfall claim is wrong. At far=1, nA and st still feed the ragged sides at 40% (nAe and ste, materials.ts:1631-1632), so only nB, 1 read of 5, can be skipped. Far sheets are small on screen anyway, so drop that part. (3) The far reads hit tiny, cached mips, so the saving is mostly sampler issue rate: about 0.2-0.7 ms on a weak integrated GPU in wide range views, not 0.5-2. textureGrad can be slightly slower than implicit reads on near pixels. (4) Reflections: turning detail off is fine for the pond pass (1/2 to 1/3 resolution, ripples, f0 0.05). It is not fine for High's mirror cube (512 px faces, bronze f0 0.8, a 30 m parallax sphere reflecting the paved dais). Keep detail there on High.
verdicts.correctedSaving: About 6 texture reads per rock pixel past 150 m, 2 per ground pixel past 140 m, and 2-3 more past 260-320 m. Roughly 0.2-0.7 ms on a weak integrated GPU in wide range views. Waterfalls: 1 read, negligible. Pond reflection pass: up to about 6-8 reads per near rock texel.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None in the main view. Detail off in reflections only for the pond pass (and Mid's mirror), not for High's mirror cube.

verdicts.reason: The header finding is confirmed. I ran curl -I today: gate.glb.gz and manifest.json both return 'public, max-age=0, must-revalidate' with an ETag and X-Vercel-Cache HIT. next.config.ts is empty and there is no vercel.json. GLBs are fetched with the default cache mode (assets.ts:313), so each use is a conditional 304 round trip to the edge. The JSON files use cache:'no-cache' (assets.ts:139) and would need versioned names too. Corrections: (1) The early start cannot be a static <link rel=preload> in the HTML. Save-Data and ?view=page visitors never download the scene (sect-client.tsx:24-29), and browsers without WebGL2 or DecompressionStream fall back (sect-experience.tsx:207-209). Chunk files also differ by tier (filesLow on phones and Low) and by the stop a deep link starts at. Only the tier-independent files are safe to start early: the manifest, camera/meta/clouds JSON, and the backdrop (globalLow is null, so it is the same 9.6 MB for every tier). Start them from a tiny inline script that checks the same conditions, like the existing POSTER_SCRIPT, and hand the responses to the loader. (2) The 25-30 revalidations are spread over the whole flight, because the streamer loads one area at a time (streaming.ts:38). Only about 4-8 are on the opening path. (3) Phone browser caches may evict 100+ MB of GLBs, so repeat-visit gains on phones are smaller. Needs content-hashed or version-folder names from sect_pack.py, a headers() rule, and the inline script. That is M, not S.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Load time only. Repeat visit: about 4-8 round trips off the opening path (roughly 0.2-0.6 s on mobile), with the rest saved quietly during the flight. First visit: the manifest, JSON and backdrop start roughly 0.5-1 s earlier. That is about 5% of a 20 MB opening download on a 10 Mbps phone.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None, if rebakes always produce new names and manifest.json stays no-cache. A badly targeted preload would waste 8-11 MB on phones, Save-Data and page-view visitors.

verdicts.reason: Mostly already done offline, and the proposal misses that. Before the bake, Blender decimates terrain weighted by distance to the camera path (BIG_RATIO 0.3). The range gets full detail only near a view. Heavy pieces are split by face distance, and distant pieces under 6 px on screen are dropped (bake_web.py:91-99, 170-180). After the bake, sect_pack.py runs a meshopt pass that keeps UV seams. It simplifies every area primitive to under 0.5 px of error at 1080 lines at its nearest approach to the camera path (sect_pack.py:646-649, 840-905). So far geometry is not unsimplified. Other errors: 'every tier draws the same triangles' contradicts the cited 4.74M (Low) vs 6.66M (High). globalLow null refers to a 2048 px texture copy of the backdrop, not geometry. What is really left: (a) the backdrop and *_trees files skip the packer's sub-pixel pass (simp only for area_ids, sect_pack.py:1706-1709). Running the same pass on backdrop.glb is a re-pack, invisible by construction, with no second copy and no extra download. Check first why it was left out, given the carried normals and the proxies. (b) A runtime per-stop LOD for neighbouring areas seen from hundreds of metres, which carry detail sized for their own nearest approach. The ladder's standIns step (backdrop proxies) is the extreme form of that LOD. Timing the gate with standIns on and off using the GPU timer gives an upper bound before building anything.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Unknown, and bounded above by what the standIns step saves at the gate (measure it). The first step, the backdrop through the existing sub-pixel pass, saves some of its 1.48M triangles with no extra download. The full runtime LOD costs about 20-30% more geometry bytes.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None if the error bound stays under 0.5 px at each cell's nearest camera distance for the stops where it is used, with UV seams kept, as the packer already does.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed that Low has no sun haze or vignette anywhere. They exist only in effects.ts. PlainRender draws the world and then the overlay into the default framebuffer (scene.tsx:1702-1715), so a third draw stays in the same tile pass. The formula claim is wrong, though. High adds the haze in linear light, scaled down by (1 - 0.7 x luma of the pixel) (effects.ts:76-78), and Low's framebuffer holds sRGB-encoded colour. 'ONE, SRC_ALPHA: dst = haze + dst*vignette' drops that luminance scaling. Bright surfaces toward the sun would then get the full glow and clip per channel to yellow-white, which High avoids. Better: a screen blend (ONE, ONE_MINUS_SRC_COLOR) for the haze, which lifts darks and spares brights the way High does and never clips. Then a multiply quad (ZERO, SRC_COLOR) for the vignette, with its factor raised to about 1/2.2 for encoded space. That is two cheap draws. Dither the haze quad's own output: the glow is a broad gradient on an 8-bit buffer, and Low dithers only inside materials (glsl.ts:466-490). The cost is lower than claimed: about 40 ops on a phone at about 0.75 MP is tiny.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Not a saving. Costs about 0.1-0.3 ms on a mid phone for two blended full-screen draws in the same render pass.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: A visible gain on Low, close to High's haze and vignette but not identical (encoded-space approximation). Bloom, cloud shade and the hue clip are still missing.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed that Medium has no anti-aliasing at 1x. Mid has msaa 0 (runtime.ts:200), the canvas antialias flag is set only when there is no post pass (scene.tsx:2370), and Mid tree cards fall back from alpha-to-coverage (sect-experience.tsx:532). Low actually has native canvas MSAA. Mid on touch and on Safari runs at 1.5x, which helps there. Corrections: (1) A second EffectPass is right. A convolution effect merged into the current pass would sample the pass's input, the HDR image before haze, bloom and clip. But the order should be hue clip, then FXAA in pass 2, then dither. The dither moves out of pass 1 to the end of pass 2, because it must stay last. Running FXAA after the dither, as proposed, would blur the dither. (2) No new full-size target is needed. The EffectComposer already keeps two ping-pong buffers. The cost is one more full-screen read and write of the half-float buffer plus FXAA's maths. (3) Turn it on only when msaa is 0, so High never pays at its top quality. After the ladder drops High's MSAA it pays a little back, still cheaper than MSAA. The pipeline is already rebuilt when MSAA changes (runtime.ts climbRebuildsPipeline), so switching is free to wire in. Use FXAA's edge threshold so fine baked texture detail is left mostly alone.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Not a saving. About 0.3-0.8 ms on an integrated GPU at 1080p (FXAA plus one extra full-screen half-float pass). No extra render target.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: A visible gain on Medium edges and tree cards. FXAA softens fine baked detail slightly (SMAA less so).

verdicts.reason: The cost is real. In three r186 MeshBasicMaterial runs map, then color, then alphamap, then alphatest, so the grade, foliage range, canopy vary and the 16-slot sectRangeW loop all run before the card discard. This happens on every tier. The saving is overstated, though. A GPU only skips work when every pixel in a block (a 2x2 quad, and really a 32-64 lane group) is cut out. In mixed blocks the discarded lanes just wait. Sprite crowns have clean transparent corners, so whole blocks drop there. Needle fans mix 1-3 px needles with 1-3 px gaps, so most blocks stay mixed. The driver may also already move the rgb-only grade below the discard. Corrections: (1) Keep the twig detail multiply after the grade. Today cardAlphaMapGlsl applies it inside alphamap_fragment, which runs after color_fragment. The grade is non-linear, so running the twig multiply before it changes colours. (2) For sprites, the decision can sit right after map_fragment plus the boost and fade. Needle and twig cards need the grade moved below alphatest_fragment. (3) The grade has no derivatives, so moving it after the discard is safe. fwidth and the mip derivatives already run earlier. (4) A surer, separate win: compute sectRangeW per vertex for card materials. Cards are a few metres across and the weight fades over 25 m (range-look.ts:37), so the loop leaves every card pixel, kept or discarded, with no visible change. Measure the change with the existing GPU timer at the gate or range.
codeRefs: three r186 ShaderLib/meshbasic.glsl.js fragment order: map, color, alphamap, alphatest
verdicts.correctedSaving: About 10-30% of card-fragment work, not 35-50%. The cap is how many pixel blocks are fully cut out: good on sprite crowns, poor on needle fans. Guess 0.2-1 ms on an integrated GPU or phone in forest-heavy views. Moving sectRangeW to the vertex shader removes about 100-160 ops from every card pixel, whether it is kept or discarded.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None, if the twig detail multiply stays after the grade and the alpha-to-coverage sharpening (sectPx with fwidth) still runs before the discard.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. pulse means hovered, focused or selected (scene.tsx:1925), and continuous includes it, so with maxFps 0 the loop goes to 'always' (1929-1936). Every pointermove also wakes 200 ms (1173-1183), so any mouse motion over the canvas at rest renders at the screen's full rate. The glow is 0.75+0.25*sin(3.2t), about 0.5 Hz (1430). The pick is throttled to 50 ms (1408). Corrections: (1) Do not render these frames through the existing capped branch, render(now, true). Driver's useFrame counts capped frames as moving (1967) and gives the ladder their 33 ms intervals with capMs 0 (2009-2011). On browsers without the GPU timer (Safari, Firefox), the ladder would read 33 ms as over the 20 ms budget and step quality down (runtime.ts:434-436). Render them as idle frames from the idle branch, render(now, false). (2) Hover and drag share store.wakeUntil. FreeLookInput's drag also calls wake(store, 250) (scene.tsx:319). The hover wake needs its own field, so drag-look keeps the full rate. (3) The lore card that follows the cursor is positioned inside useFrame (1423). At 30 renders a second it would update about every 66 ms instead of every 50 ms. Position it from the pointermove handler instead. (4) Optional: render a short full-rate burst (about 300 ms) when hovered changes, so the damp-10 fade-in (1432) stays smooth. Nothing else reads the pointer for visuals: no parallax.
verdicts.correctedSaving: As stated while the mouse moves or rests on a hotspot. A 60 Hz screen draws 50% fewer frames, a 144 Hz screen about 79% fewer. This counts only once the ladder bug above is avoided.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None. Idle motion during hover drops to the 30 fps it already has at rest. The lore card needs DOM positioning to keep its 20 Hz follow.

verdicts.reason: The blur declarations are where the proposal says, with no tier switch. But two of the targets cost nothing per frame. The map and readers set store.modal (sect-experience.tsx:1204-1207), and then the scene does not redraw (scene.tsx:1948), so their blur is not recomputed. The page-view header (content.css:1674-1676) sits over the opaque page view while the 3D view is paused (sect-experience.tsx:1220), so its blur only reruns on scroll. Drop both from the list. The real per-frame targets are two. First, the area panel: .sect-panel.sc-panel is 0.895 opaque, and paper.webp has an alpha channel, so it adds a little more cover. Removing its blur on every tier is near-invisible. Second, the always-visible HUD plates (sect.css:375-380), used by about 8 controls in overlay.tsx and sound-toggle.tsx. Removing their blur on Low is a visible Low-only change, which the owner's rule does not cover, so it is the owner's call. Gate it by a tier class on the root, not a coarse-pointer media query, or High-tier tablets change too. Each backdrop-filter element makes the compositor copy what is behind it into its own pass whenever the canvas updates. On tiled phone GPUs that costs more than the pixel count suggests. The idle rate is 30, or 20 after 20 s.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Guess 0.2-1 ms of compositor GPU per redrawn frame on phones, mostly from the area panel. Not profiled. The map, readers and page-view header save nothing.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None for the area panel. On Low, the plates would show a sharper scene through their 18% see-through. Owner's call.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. On Low, three's colorspace_fragment encodes to sRGB, then the fog chunk decodes gl_FragColor and fogColor, fogs, clips and encodes again (glsl.ts:485-490). three uploads fogColor in the output colour space when drawing to the screen, so it really does arrive encoded. The count is off. Today a fogged pixel runs 12 pow calls (three's encode 3, the decode 3, the fogColor decode 3, the final encode 3), and each pow is log2 plus exp2. After both steps only the final 3 remain, so 9 are removed, not 6. Step 1 removes 3. Step 2 removes 6: three's encode and the decode that undoes it. Step 1 may save nothing on drivers that already pull uniform-only maths out of the per-pixel code (Qualcomm does), but it costs nothing to do. Implementation: change it once in installFog (materials.ts:81-91). Make colorspace_fragment skip its encode under USE_FOG, drop the decode at glsl.ts:486, and pass a linear copy of the fog colour as its own uniform. Audit the custom shaders that include colorspace_fragment (materials.ts 1193, 1308, 1439, 1501, 1673, 1909, 1978; flames, fx, life, grass, waterfall-fx). Those checked put fog_fragment straight after it. Sky shaders that use SCREEN_DITHER_GLSL without three's fog are not affected. Mid and High draw into the composer's linear buffer, so nothing changes there.
verdicts.correctedSaving: 9 of 12 pow calls per fogged pixel on Low, about 18 special-function ops. Low frames are mostly limited by memory bandwidth and fill, so guess 2-5% of a Low frame's GPU time, not 5-10%.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None. The same float maths and the same clip and dither run on the same values.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. The useLayoutEffect at scene.tsx:1518-1546 disposes and rebuilds the composer whenever quality.msaa, quality.bloom, cloudShadows or holdFocus change. Step-downs happen mid-flight. Climbs that rebuild already wait for the camera to rest (runtime.ts:308-316, scene.tsx:2013-2016), so half of this is already mitigated. Corrections: (1) holdFocus also flips. atmosFeatures ties holdFocus to now.msaa > 0 and cloudShadows to now.bloom (post.ts:29-35). So the MSAA-to-0 step also rebuilds to remove hold focus, and hold focus needs a switch-off by uniform as well. (2) composer.multisampling already has a setter in postprocessing 6.39 (build/index.js:985). It only disposes the two buffers, which reallocate on the next render: a small hitch of a few ms, not a shader compile. (3) The MSAA-to-0 step also recompiles the tree card programs (setCardCoverageOf sets needsUpdate, assets.ts:1302-1307), so pre-compiling those variants matters. (4) Bloom switched off by uniform still costs one texture read per pixel in the merged shader. bloom.update must also be skipped. (5) Which steps it covers: up to 3 stalls on auto High (4 to 2 samples when DPR < 1.25, 2 to 0, bloom off) and 1 on Medium (bloom, which also removes cloud shadows).
verdicts.correctedSaving: Removes the shader-compile stall on each mid-flight step-down (up to 3 on auto High, 1 on Medium). The guessed 30-150 ms each is plausible next to the repo's own 18-40 ms and 46 ms notes. A few ms of buffer reallocation stays at each MSAA change. Climbs could then happen in flight.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None, if bloom, cloud shadow and hold focus switched off by uniform match today's removed passes. The cost is one extra texture read per pixel at the bottom steps.

verdicts.reason: No KTX2 or Basis code exists, and the manifest confirms the memory figures. Full-set decoded textures with mips total about 2.12 GiB, and the Low set about 0.70 GiB. Dividing GPU memory by 4 is right, since BC7 and ASTC 4x4 are 8 bits per pixel against 32 for RGBA. Corrections: (1) The download grows more than claimed. UASTC is 8 bits per pixel before supercompression, so the full set is about 530 MiB as UASTC. After RDO plus zstd it is roughly 200-320 MB, against about 40 MB of WebP today (full minus low bytes is about 2.8 MB per area). Area files go from about 11 MB to about 25-40 MB, 2.5-3.5 times, not about double. That breaks the packer's ~10 MB per chunk budget. (2) The steady-state CPU copy is already freed: prepare.ts:320-331 closes each ImageBitmap after upload. So only the GPU memory and the in-flight decode peak are saved. (3) The grass root read samples atlases through a shader into a render target (grass.tsx:414-459), so it still works with compressed textures. (4) It adds the Basis transcoder (WASM in workers) and transcode time on phones. Older devices without ASTC fall back to ETC2. Trial one area for bytes, PSNR and a side-by-side look. Consider the cheaper fallback (decode each WebP just before its upload) first.
verdicts.correctedSaving: GPU texture memory divided by 4: about 1.23 GB to 0.31 GB at the forge on desktop Medium and High. Uploads move about 4 times less data, with no mip generation. Download cost: textures about 40 MB to about 200-320 MB over the flight, and area files 2.5-3.5 times larger.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: None expected with UASTC (no RDO, or a low RDO setting) encoded from the original PNG bakes. It may even beat today's WebP q88, which halves colour resolution. ETC1S would band baked light. The real cost is download size and load time on slow connections.

verdicts.reason: The 0.75 step is plain browser upscaling (runtime.ts:208-213), and keepLook tiers can reach it (runtime.ts:253-261). But FSR 1 needs anti-aliased input. By the 0.75 step, auto tiers have already dropped MSAA (runtime.ts:256-260), Medium never has it (runtime.ts:200), and the pipeline has no FXAA or SMAA (effects.ts:192-231). On that input, the edge-aware upscale plus sharpen would sharpen stair-steps and the shimmer of needles and grass in motion. Only a visitor-picked High tier still has MSAA at that step. Also, the DitherEffect runs at the end of the merged pass (effects.ts:217-218). It must move after the upscale, or the sharpen boosts the dither noise. The cost guess is low for the weak integrated GPUs that actually reach this step: more like 0.5-1.5 ms at 1080p. That is small against the 26 ms frame, but it can delay climbs. Recommendation: gate FSR to msaa > 0, or use the sharpen pass alone on today's upscale. Then measure before adding finer steps.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Not a saving. It adds an estimated 0.5-1.5 ms on the integrated GPUs that reach the step, plus one full-size buffer.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: A clear gain only where the input has MSAA (visitor-picked High). On Medium and auto tiers without MSAA it can make jaggies and shimmer more visible, unless an anti-aliasing pass is added.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed that grassTier returns 'off' without post (grass.ts:220-226) and that Low's canvas requests antialias (scene.tsx:2370). Browsers usually give 4x MSAA, but it is not guaranteed. Problems: (1) A 40 m reach misses the lawns the holds actually frame, 50-110 m out (grass.ts:130-133). The visible gain would mostly come mid-flight, not at the stops where visitors rest. (2) It adds cost on the weakest devices. That means GPU time, the main-thread build in 6 ms slices (grass.tsx:671-686), and a GPU readback per atlas (readRoots, grass.tsx:414-459) on phones. It does not fit the owner's 'same cost' rule. (3) The GPU guess is low: Mid's 0.05 ms for 16k tufts on an RTX 5080, on a phone GPU 20-50 times slower, gives about 0.3-1 ms for a near layer, and near tufts cover the most pixels. Revision: make Low grass a ladder rung. It turns on only while frames have headroom and is the first thing dropped. Give it a reach that covers the hold lawns, about 80-110 m at low density.
verdicts.correctedSaving: Not a saving. Estimated 0.3-1 ms of phone GPU, plus main-thread build and a GPU readback per area. Acceptable only when gated on ladder headroom.
verdicts.correctedQualityCost: A visible gain on Low only if the reach covers the hold lawns. At 40 m it shows mostly in flight.

verdicts.reason: The proposal admits a visible loss on Low and Medium: steppier water, flames and petals, and 12 fps reads as stutter. The owner's rule allows only no-loss savings or changes that bring Low and Medium closer to High. The saving is also overstated, because the code already dims to 20 fps after 20 s (scene.tsx:1729-1731, 1949). Counted over a whole rest, the proposal cuts rendered frames by about 17% over 10 s, 25% over 20 s, 11% over 60 s and 24% over 2 minutes. That is nowhere near half. A no-loss alternative for every tier: dim when the window has lost focus (blur, or document.hasFocus() false). The visitor is not looking then.

observations: Mid and High draw almost the same geometry (gate: 6.48M vs 6.66M tris; forge: 5.12M vs 5.26M). Almost all of that difference is grass. The gap between tiers is mostly texture size, grass and reflection resolution, not mesh detail.

Triangle counts are very high everywhere: the gate view draws 4.7M (low) to 6.7M (high) triangles. Each area is 1.0-2.1M triangles, plus about 1.48M global triangles (backdrop). Triangles actually drawn are far fewer than resident triangles (gate low: 4.7M drawn vs 5.5M resident; forge mid: 5.1M drawn vs 10.7M resident), so the view frustum is culling a lot. Even so 3-5M triangles per frame is the main cost for weak GPUs.

Draw calls are 73-545 and vary a lot by place: gate is the heaviest (303 low, 482 mid, 545 high), summit the lightest (73/105/117). Gate has the most calls because it shows the most distinct meshes. Merging or instancing at the gate and forge would help most.

Texture memory is the largest number. Per-area decoded texBytes is 168-286 MB on mid/high versus 63-91 MB on low (about 2.7x smaller). Mid/high hold 4-6 areas resident, about 780 MB to 1.23 GB of GPU texture memory; low holds 3-4 areas, about 200-280 MB. The forge stop on mid/high keeps 6 areas resident, which is the memory peak and is risky for phones and integrated GPUs. Mid appears to use the same 4096 texture set as high (texBytes identical), so mid saves nothing on textures versus high. Mid's saving is only in grass and reflection resolution.

Because texBytes are decoded RGBA estimates and textures are WebP-in-GLB, GPU memory is roughly 4 bytes per pixel with no compression. A GPU-compressed format (KTX2/BC7/ASTC) would cut this about 4-8x for mid/high with the same visuals; this is a candidate for idea (a). The streamed download size is small (6.6-12.9 MB per area), so the cost is decoded size, not network.

Grass is the only live effect that differs sharply by tier. High at the gate draws 35,824 instances / 322k tris; mid draws 9,750 / 88k; low draws 0 (grass tier off). High generates about 4x more candidate blades than mid (gate 184k vs 41k candidates, 69k vs 23k built instances), and High keeps 215-329k instances resident. Low has no grass at all, so Low looks visibly barer than High. A cheap grass layer (a few thousand instances or baked grass cards) on Low would close the look gap (idea b). Grass CPU time is tiny (0.05-0.16 ms), so the cost is GPU triangle count, not CPU.
Mid-tier grass drops from 9,750 to 255 instances between gate and summit, and High drops from 35,824 to 7,218, so grass cost is concentrated at gate, mirror and forge.

Shader programs: 43-48 on low, 53-58 on mid, 55-60 on high. That is a moderate count; the extra programs on mid/high are mostly for grass, reflections and post effects. Not a big lever on its own, but program compile at first view causes hitches on slow devices; precompiling or warming programs during the loader would hide that.

Reflections: mid reflects at roughly 996x983 and high at roughly 1245x1229 (about 1.25x per axis) at the gate; at forge and summit the drawing size was 0x0 (nothing reflective in view), so the reflection cost is paid only where water is visible. Low's reflection state was not captured in the truncated output.
Flames are enabled on all three tiers (forge flame sources present on low), so fire effects are not tier-gated.
Stream status was clean: loading and failed lists were empty at every place after about 6 s, ready/drawn true for every resident area; no load errors seen.
Console showed 0 errors and 8 warnings (log saved at .playwright-mcp/console-2026-11-04T18-14-44-939Z.log); I did not read the warnings.

Frames were taken from camera.json holds: gate 93, mirror 217, forge 352, arena 516, mission 619, library 772, steles 974, scroll 1103, formation 1208, abode 1380, summit 1647. I measured gate, forge and summit.
problems: The browser had a real RTX 5080 GPU (not SwiftShader), so these counts are from a strong machine. The tier was forced with ?tier=, so counts show what each tier draws, not how a weak device would behave. No frame times were read, so GPU cost per tier is not measured.

__sectPost and __sectReflect output was truncated to 200 characters and mostly returned frustum plane data; I did not get post-processing settings (bloom, MSAA, render scale) or Low's reflection state. The Low-tier runs did not return a reflect or post value at all (the fields were missing from the output).

The 6-second settle may not be enough for the grass builder in every case (grass 'building' was 0 in all runs, so it did finish), and the Low tier's grass 'off' is by design, not a loading failure.
