webTechniques.name: KTX2 / Basis Universal textures (UASTC for baked lightmaps, ETC1S for the rest)
webTechniques.support: KTX2Loader is in three since r129 and works on r186 (the site's r0.186). Needs WebGL2/WASM. ASTC is on nearly all phones and Apple GPUs; BC7 on desktop; ETC2 on older Android. Open issue #34389: the bundled transcoder needs CSP 'unsafe-eval'. The KTX-Software 4.4.x and basis_universal 2.50 encoders are current.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Best single fit and the biggest win. It is the one lever that cuts memory (the likely cause of iOS tab kills) and upload stalls on every tier with no visible change if UASTC is used for lightmap-like atlases. It is a build-time change (gltf-transform uastc/etc1s or toktx) and the Low 2048 set could shrink further. Cost: bigger downloads than lossy WebP at equal quality (UASTC with zstd is larger than WebP), so test per chunk. WebP can stay for tiny or distant textures. Risks: alpha edges and normal-less baked data are fine; check sRGB flag.

webTechniques.name: Texture memory budget and eviction (drop decoded/high mips for far areas; avoid mipmap-less filters)
webTechniques.support: Plain three.js (texture.dispose, renderer.info.memory). iOS Safari jetsam kills the web process at a per-process limit; one iOS 26 report shows a 2048 MB limit and a crash with about 1.48 GB resident.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: The ladder already steps down detail but the research shows the real crash risk on phones is resident texture bytes, not frame time. A hard texture-byte budget by deviceMemory/iOS (for example 800 MB-1 GB) checked via renderer.info and the manifest texBytes would be cheap insurance. Pairs well with KTX2 so the budget stretches 4x.

webTechniques.name: FSR 1 style upscaling (EASU + RCAS) after a lower render scale
webTechniques.support: Pure WebGL2 fragment shaders; runs anywhere. three r184+ has built-in nodes for WebGPURenderer; for WebGLRenderer a custom ShaderPass of the MIT-licensed shader works. Needs a full-screen pass, so it adds one extra render-to-texture on phones.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Directly improves option (b): today the 0.75 render-scale rung uses plain browser scaling. Replacing that with EASU+RCAS makes Low/Medium look closer to High at the same pixel cost, and also lets Medium run at 0.8-0.85 scale with sharper output. Cost: one more pass and one more full-resolution target, which matters on bandwidth-limited phones; skip it when render scale is 1.

webTechniques.name: Temporal AA / TAAU instead of MSAA on the heaviest tiers
webTechniques.support: Works in WebGL2 with a custom or postprocessing pass; three r184 added a TAAU node for WebGPURenderer. Not built into WebGLRenderer.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Only partly fits. MSAA is already the cheaper-looking choice for this baked, mostly static look and the ladder already drops it first. A cheap variant is SMAA/FXAA (one pass, no history) for Low when MSAA is off, so edges stay clean for the upscaler. Full TAA is a bigger risk because of the animated live touches; consider it only for static shots and scroll rest.

webTechniques.name: Half-resolution bloom and other quarter-cost post effects
webTechniques.support: Works in WebGL2 today; postprocessing 6.x already uses a mip-chain based bloom and supports a resolution scale on effects. three UnrealBloomPass also takes a resolution.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Cheap, safe win for Medium and Low: the ladder drops bloom entirely as a late step, so a half-res bloom that costs a quarter as much would keep bloom on longer. Check the existing postprocessing setup to see whether bloom is already half-res before counting on this; it is the first thing to verify.

webTechniques.name: Compute Pressure API (CPU/thermal pressure signal)
webTechniques.support: Chrome and Edge 125+ on desktop only; not Chrome for Android, not Firefox, not Safari (caniuse: about 27% global usage, March 2026 data). Only the 'cpu' source exists. Feature-detect with 'PressureObserver' in globalThis.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Low value for the weak-device goal: phones, the main target, are not covered, and this scene is GPU-bound. Possible as a tiny desktop-laptop extra (a laptop on battery, thermally throttled) feeding the existing ladder as a second input. Not worth building first.

webTechniques.name: Battery Status, Save-Data, reduced-motion and low-power signals as tier hints
webTechniques.support: Battery Status: Chrome/Edge/Opera/Samsung/Chrome Android only; removed in Firefox 52, never in Safari (iOS has no battery API and no JS flag for Low Power Mode). Save-Data / navigator.connection: Chromium only. prefers-reduced-motion: all major browsers. deviceMemory is Chromium only (capped at 8).
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Partial fit. chooseTier already uses touch, deviceMemory and cores. Adding saveData and battery (not charging and under about 20%) as 'start one tier lower, 30 fps cap' is cheap on Android. iOS low-power mode cannot be detected directly; one indirect tell is that Safari drops requestAnimationFrame to 30 Hz, which the ladder's frame-time measure already sees. prefers-reduced-motion should reduce camera easing and live particle motion, which is also an accessibility gain.

webTechniques.name: Parallel shader compile: renderer.compileAsync and KHR_parallel_shader_compile
webTechniques.support: KHR_parallel_shader_compile is in Chrome, Edge and Firefox on most hardware, and Safari. The three.js compileAsync API is stable on WebGLRenderer.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Fits well because the site streams chunks with custom live shaders (grass, flames, water, ink): each new area can hit a first-use compile stall during the fly-through. Call compileAsync on a chunk's group before adding it to the visible scene, and warm the postprocessing passes for each ladder step. Check the existing code first, since the site may already do this.

webTechniques.name: ImageBitmap decode in workers and throttled texture uploads
webTechniques.support: createImageBitmap in workers: Chrome, Firefox, Safari (GLTFLoader historically avoided it on Safari; check the current behaviour for r186). Safari does not do ImageBitmap decode for GLTFLoader textures in older code.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: The site uses WebP inside GLB, so the browser decode runs per chunk. Staggering uploads (one texture per frame, using initTexture and a time budget of about 4-6 ms) is the cheap fix for scroll hitching as chunks arrive. This is complementary to KTX2, which removes both decode and large upload; if KTX2 lands, the staggering matters much less.

webTechniques.name: Impostors and HLOD for distant areas
webTechniques.support: Plain three.js (THREE.LOD, Sprite, custom meshes); no browser feature needed.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: The ladder already swaps other areas for stand-ins and turns tree cards off, so this is partly done. The research-backed improvement is to make the stand-in look closer to the real area (a cube or octahedral impostor baked in Cycles, which the owner's pipeline can produce offline) and use it on every tier for areas beyond the +-2 window. That cuts cost on Low and Medium without touching High's near area. Because High keeps full detail within range, this respects 'quality beats optimisation'.

webTechniques.name: BatchedMesh and InstancedMesh to cut draw calls
webTechniques.support: Plain three.js r186; BatchedMesh uses WEBGL_multi_draw where available, with a fallback.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Check ?debug=1 window.__sect.info() first: baked chunks with a few large atlases may already be low in draw calls, in which case gains are small. Where there are many small repeated props (lanterns, roof tiles, trees, rocks), instancing them with a shared baked atlas is the likely win. Note per-chunk culling still matters: do not merge across chunks.

webTechniques.name: Meshopt plus quantization and mesh simplification for far chunks
webTechniques.support: gltfpack and meshoptimizer; EXT_meshopt_compression is already supported by the loader.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Fits as option (a)/(b) for far chunks on all tiers: the ladder's stand-in step becomes a real simplified mesh rather than a card, so the look stays closer to full detail. It costs extra download size per chunk (a second GLB), so make the far copy lazy and small.

webTechniques.name: WebGPU renderer (with automatic WebGL2 fallback)
webTechniques.support: Chrome and Edge 113+ (Windows, macOS, ChromeOS), Chrome Android 12+; Safari 26 on macOS and iOS/iPadOS (since September 2025); Firefox on Windows (v141) and Apple Silicon macOS, all macOS Apple Silicon since v147; Linux and Android Firefox behind a flag. caniuse global roughly 87%. Low-end Android phones with old GPUs and old iPhones that cannot run iOS 26 stay on WebGL2.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Poor fit for the stated goal today. The scene is baked-light, fill-rate and memory bound; WebGPU does not reduce either on its own, the migration is large, and the weakest devices are exactly those that fall back to WebGL2. Revisit later for render bundles (cheap re-submission of static chunks) or compute-based grass.

webTechniques.name: iOS Safari memory ceiling: budget resident memory and fall back to fewer contexts
webTechniques.support: Apple publishes no number; limits vary by device RAM and OS version and have changed between iOS releases. Treat the figures as anecdotal.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Strong fit. With ~180-243 MB decoded per full chunk and five resident on desktop, an iPhone at 'one each side' is three chunks (about 60 MB each at Low), well under the reported ceiling, so the current phone setup looks safe. The risk is a user forcing a higher tier on a phone, or render targets (MSAA, bloom, FSR) at DPR 3. Add a memory-based guard and use KTX2 to widen the margin; test on a real older iPhone with Safari memory logging.

webTechniques.name: OffscreenCanvas: render three.js in a worker
webTechniques.support: Chrome 69+, Edge 79+, Firefox 105+, Safari 16.4+ (WebGL in workers included). Safari had historical bugs; test on iOS.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Poor value for the risk. The site is scroll-driven (scroll value can be sent to the worker cheaply), but the existing React/drei/postprocessing architecture and ?debug hooks make a port large, and the frame-time bottleneck is GPU, not main thread. Consider only for GLB parsing (a worker already used by meshopt/KTX2 decoders) rather than rendering.

webTechniques.name: Frame pacing: render only when something moves, 30 fps cap, pause offscreen/hidden
webTechniques.support: requestAnimationFrame everywhere; page visibility and IntersectionObserver everywhere. Safari throttles rAF to 30 Hz in Low Power Mode, which is a free signal. Display refresh of 90/120 Hz Android phones makes a deliberate 60 cap worthwhile.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: The ladder already has a 30 fps cap as the last step; the research suggests an earlier, softer step: cap the live-touch simulations (grass, flames, waterfalls) to 30 Hz while the camera still renders at 60 on Medium, and fully idle when the scroll is still and effects are off-screen. Also confirm rendering stops when the tab is hidden or the loading screen waits for Enter. Check current behaviour in runtime.ts before counting this as new.

webTechniques.name: Dynamic resolution done smoothly (continuous render scale, pixel-ratio caps, and render-target reuse)
webTechniques.support: Plain three.js (setPixelRatio / setSize or a scaled render target). three's WebGLRenderer reallocates on setSize.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: The existing ladder already steps resolution, MSAA and render scale. A finer render-scale control between 1.0 and 0.75 (e.g. 0.9, 0.85, 0.8) means devices that are only slightly short of 60 fps keep far more detail, which is the owner's 'quality first' principle. Low risk, no new assets.

webTechniques.name: Variable-rate shading / foveated rendering (and cheap substitutes)
webTechniques.support: No general WebGL support. WebXR foveation exists only for headsets. WebGPU has no shipped VRS feature either. Treat as unavailable.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Does not fit. The lighting is baked, so the main cost is texture sampling and overdraw, not expensive per-pixel lighting that VRS usually saves. A cheaper equivalent already in the ladder is lowering render scale; FSR-style upscaling is the better route.

webTechniques.name: Anisotropic filtering, mip bias and texture-filter tuning per tier
webTechniques.support: EXT_texture_filter_anisotropic is in all desktop browsers and nearly all phones; texture.mipmapBias exists in three r186 for the filtering bias.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Fits: the site already ships a 2048 px Low texture set, but anisotropy and mip bias are free dials per tier and make Low sharper at the same cost. Verify the current values in runtime.ts; this is a small tuning job, not a new system.

webTechniques.name: Lazy GPU resource creation: avoid duplicate decodes and keep CPU copies small
webTechniques.support: Plain three.js (ImageBitmap.close, BufferAttribute.onUpload). GLTFLoader with ImageBitmapLoader already moves decode off thread on supporting browsers.
webTechniques.fitsThisSite: Worth auditing: with chunk textures at hundreds of MB decoded, any CPU copy kept after upload is wasted memory on phones. Check by watching Chrome DevTools memory or Safari Web Inspector on an iPhone, then release in the chunk loader. Small effort, no visual change, and it widens the iOS safety margin.

mapNotes.area: Render pipeline and frame loop (Canvas setup, Driver, composer chain, reflections, quality ladder, idle logic)
mapNotes.notes:
I could not run the page (no dev server, no GPU, GLBs are LFS pointers), so every cost is an estimate from code, shader instruction counts, the manifest and numbers the repo's own comments quote; none is measured. To measure: ?debug=1, then window.__sect.info() (draw calls, triangles), window.__sectPost (same-frame pass toggles), window.__sectReflect (mode 'passes' or 'frame' GPU time), and the Driver's EXT_disjoint_timer_query timer feeding the ladder (Chrome only).

Answers to the direct questions. Scene renders per frame: Low 2 (world, overlay) straight to the canvas. Mid and High normal frames 3 draw-list submissions into the composer (RenderPass world, OverlayPass, then the final EffectPass fullscreen) plus bloom's 16 small passes and, on High at rest, hold focus's 2 half-res passes. At the Mirror area add the pond planar pass every frame and a cube face on capture frames (6 consecutive frames every 6 s), so up to 3 scene submissions a frame there. There is no separate depth prepass: the composer blits the depth into a stable 32-bit float depth texture after the RenderPass (needsDepthBlit), and soft depth for puffs, cloud shadow and hold focus read it. Targets: all half float (HalfFloatType) at the full drawing-buffer size (canvas size x dpr, dpr up to 1.5 on High, 1 on Mid unless touch or Safari-on-Mac); pond reflection 0.5 or 1/3 of the drawing buffer only over the pond's rectangle; cube 512 or 256 px per face. Composer chain pass by pass: RenderPass, OverlayPass (needsSwap false, draws into the same buffer), EffectPass(hold focus [High], cloud shadow, bloom, sun haze, vignette, hue clip, dither) to the screen, with bloom's own luminance + mip chain as sub-passes. Rest logic: the page has its own rest logic (Driver), not R3F's: demand loop, 30 fps idle, 20 fps after 20 s, 10 fps while veiled, 2 fps with reduced motion, 0 under a reader or map; the flight 'always' loop only while something moves. What the ladder turns off, in order: dpr to 1 (0.25 steps), MSAA 4->2->0, bloom (and with it cloud shadows, via atmosFeatures), render scale 0.75, other areas as stand-ins (this also turns the pond's real reflection off, 'lean'), tree cards, then the 30 fps cap. A visitor-picked tier only loses resolution. What stays on at every tier: the full triangle load of the drawn areas, the sky dome, the overlay puffs, the fog math in every shader, the 32-bit depth and blit on the composer path; no tier changes geometry. Canvas flags and shader warm-up are in the cost drivers; KHR_parallel_shader_compile is used through three's compileAsync, but the composer's own programs are not pre-warmed.

Corrections to a possible first guess: the composer's output ping-pong buffer is never rendered into here, so three should not allocate it; and the 'depth texture on every buffer' cost in postprocessing 6.39.5 is one real depth target plus one stable blit target, not three live ones. I left out ideas that look good but fight the owner's rule: lowering High's resolution cap, cutting the MSAA samples on High, a depth prepass (the shading is cheap and the load is vertex-bound, so it would add draw cost), and frame-skipping in flight. Triangle LOD and occlusion culling are the largest unexamined levers (the same 6 to 9M triangles are submitted on every tier), but they belong to the asset-side areas, not this one."

drivers.what: World pass: every drawn area's baked meshes, merged per material and spatial cell (150 m cells within 250 m of the camera path, 450 m to 900 m, 1800 m beyond). Global set is 1.48M tris; each area chunk is 1.06M to 2.13M tris (manifest.json). Desktop keeps current area plus two each side drawn, so roughly 5 areas, about 6 to 9M triangles in the draw list before cell culling. There is no occlusion culling and no triangle LOD: Low, Mid and High draw the same geometry (only textures differ on Low).
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/prepare.ts:825-899 (merge by material+cell), client/src/lib/sect/cells.ts:15-21, scene.tsx:905-925 (World useFrame sets visibility per set)
drivers.when: per frame, every render
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same triangles on every tier. Only the ladder's 'stand-ins' step (runtime.ts:262, scene.tsx:913-918) draws just the camera's own area at full detail and shows the others as backdrop proxies. Phones/Low keep 1 area each side instead of 2 (streaming, not render).
drivers.costGuess: Probably the biggest single GPU item on integrated GPUs (vertex and draw-call bound, shading is a cheap baked texture plus fog). Not measured. Estimate: 2 to 6 ms of a 20 to 40 ms integrated-GPU frame (the repo comments say 720p vs 1080p cut a weak iGPU frame from 43 to 26 ms, so most of it is pixel cost, not vertex). Check draw calls and triangles with window.__sect.info() under ?debug=1.

drivers.what: Composer's main colour buffer: half-float RGBA16F (8 B/px) at the full canvas size, MSAA 2 or 4 samples on High, none on Mid, plus a 32-bit float depth texture, a second 'stable' depth target filled by a blitFramebuffer each frame, and a depth texture on the ping-pong output buffer. postprocessing 6.39.5 createDepthTexture/blitDepthBuffer. The output ping-pong buffer is never drawn into here (RenderPass and OverlayPass have needsSwap false, EffectPass goes to screen), so three should never allocate it on the GPU.
drivers.when: allocated on pipeline creation and on every resize or dpr change; depth blit and MSAA resolve every frame
drivers.tierBehaviour: High: 2 samples at dpr>=1.25, else 4 (runtime.ts:204-205), dpr up to 1.5. Mid: 0 samples, dpr 1 (1.5 on touch or Safari-on-Mac). Low: no composer. Ladder lowers dpr by 0.25 steps to 1, then msaa 4->2->0, then 0.75 render scale.
drivers.costGuess: Memory, my arithmetic, unmeasured: High at 1080p x1.5 (2880x1620, 4.67 Mpx) with 2 samples is about 60 B/px = 280 MB; with 4 samples about 85 B/px = 400 MB. Mid at 1080p x1 (2.07 Mpx) about 40 B/px = 85 MB. Counted: colour RT 8 (+8 per sample), depth 4 (+4 per sample), stable depth 4, bloom luminance 8, bloom mips about 5, canvas back buffer 4+4. Each frame also pays an MSAA resolve of colour and depth and a depth blit (about 0.1 to 0.4 ms on High, a guess).

drivers.what: Overlay pass: one instanced draw of up to about 1021 cloud puffs (clouds.json has 1021, packPuffs keeps those within 2600 m of the path), plus mist, waterfall spray, light beams, formation barrier. Each puff is a camera-facing sprite sized to an ellipsoid silhouette with 2 noise fetches, soft-depth fetch, fog math (sectHazeDepth, sectCloudDepth, exp) and no depth write. Heavy overdraw when the camera is inside a bank (the opening flight). The puff mesh has frustumCulled=false and is re-sorted far-to-near on the CPU and re-uploaded (about 53 KB) whenever the camera moves more than RESORT_DISTANCE.
drivers.where: scene.tsx:596-670 (CloudPuffs, 626 frustumCulled false, sort useFrame), materials.ts:1797-1925 (puff shader), effects.ts:137-158 (OverlayPass)
drivers.when: per frame; fill-rate cost scales with screen pixels times layers
drivers.tierBehaviour: High and Mid: full, with soft edges against geometry (reads the stable depth texture). Low: puffs without soft depth, and 'mist.*' puffs removed (scene.tsx:2327), drawn by a second gl.render with autoClear off (scene.tsx:1708-1713). Not touched by any ladder step except resolution.
drivers.costGuess: Unknown; commonly 10 to 25% of a frame in cloud-heavy views on weak GPUs. Estimate from shader size: about 70 ALU + 3 fetches per fragment per layer, 3 to 6 average layers at the gate and opening -> 0.5 to 2 ms at 1080p on an iGPU. Measure with window.__sectPost (toggle) and the frame GPU timer.

drivers.what: Final merged EffectPass (one fullscreen draw): hold focus mix (High only, depth read), cloud shadows (depth -> world position via two mat4 multiplies, 3-octave value noise = 12 hash evaluations, then two haze/cloud transmittance calls with exp), bloom add, sun haze (normalize + 2 pow), vignette, hue-preserving clip, dither (sRGB encode/decode). Cloud-shadow noise and fog transmittance are computed for every non-sky pixel even where no cloud shade falls (cover threshold 0.5 to 0.74 leaves roughly half the deck clear).
drivers.when: per rendered frame, per pixel
drivers.tierBehaviour: cloudShadows = post && bloom (lib/sect/post.ts:29-35): on for High and Mid; dropped when the ladder turns bloom off. holdFocus = High only (msaa>0 on both ceiling and current). Low: none of this runs.
drivers.costGuess: Estimated 250 to 400 flops/px, mostly cloud shadow. At 2.07 Mpx that is 0.5 to 0.8 GFLOP/frame, about 1.5 to 3 ms on a UHD 620-class iGPU (peak math, then x1.5 to 2 for real efficiency), about 0.1 to 0.2 ms on a discrete GPU. Estimated from instruction counts, not timed.

drivers.what: Bloom: mipmap blur chain. A full-resolution luminance prefilter (RGBA16F target, custom glowPrefilter), then 8 down passes starting at half res and 7 up passes, 16 small fullscreen draws in total.
drivers.when: per rendered frame (also on idle frames at rest)
drivers.tierBehaviour: High and Mid on. Ladder step 3 turns it off (and cloud shadows with it); visitor-picked tiers never lose it (keepLook).
drivers.costGuess: About 1.3 to 1.5 full-res passes of bandwidth: the full-res luminance pass (reads 8 B, writes 8 B per px) plus the chain (about 1/3 of full res total). Estimated 0.4 to 1 ms on an iGPU at 1080p, 0.1 ms discrete. About 16 draw calls of CPU overhead. Estimate, not timed.

drivers.what: Hold focus blur (High only): Kawase VERY_SMALL blur at reduced resolution, run every frame while weight>0 (that means every idle frame once resting at a stop for 0.6 s, since weight stays at 1).
drivers.when: every frame at rest at a stop on High
drivers.tierBehaviour: High only; off after the ladder drops MSAA.
drivers.costGuess: About 2 half-res passes, 0.1 to 0.3 ms on a discrete GPU. Small, but it is paid on every idle frame.

drivers.what: Pond planar reflection: a second render of the scene from a mirrored camera into a half-float target (0.5 texel/px on High, 1/3 on Mid, over the pond's screen rectangle only), with soft depth off, no grass, other areas as backdrop stand-ins. Renders EVERY frame while the Still Pond is on screen and within 320 m (no temporal throttle, also at rest).
drivers.when: every rendered frame while at the Mirror area (stops 'mirror' and nearby, frames about 1 to 916 of need range, close to the pond)
drivers.tierBehaviour: High and Mid; none on Low; skipped when ladder is on stand-ins (lean, index.ts:132). Memory about 14 MB at 1440x810 reflection size, freed away from the mirror (index.ts:111).
drivers.costGuess: A second full draw list submission (global set + mirror area + proxies), vertex and CPU bound: estimated 15 to 35% of a main world pass, 1 to 4 ms on an iGPU, plus the fill of the pond rectangle at half or third res.

drivers.what: Heart-Mirror cube probe: one cube face per frame, 6 consecutive frames for each capture, first capture on approach within 250 m, then every 6 s while within 160 m and on screen (so forever while resting at its stop 66 to 90 m away), and again whenever the set of drawn areas changes. High: 512 px faces, grass included, all areas at full detail. Mid: 256 px, no grass, stand-ins. HalfFloat cube with mip generation on the last face.
drivers.when: 6 heavy frames every 6 s at the mirror stop, 6 frames on first approach
drivers.tierBehaviour: High and Mid; none on Low. Cube memory about 17 MB (High) and 4 MB (Mid).
drivers.costGuess: Each capture frame is a third full-scene submission (about 1 world pass of triangles for High, about 30% for Mid). Average load is small (about 1 face/second); the cost is six hitch frames every 6 s at 30 fps idle (frame time roughly doubles for 0.2 s). Estimated.

drivers.what: Frame loop and idle logic: the page does not draw continuously at rest. Driver runs its own rAF; frameloop stays 'demand'. It switches to 'always' when scroll/flight/drag/hover/wake is active. At rest it renders the FULL frame (composer, overlay, reflections) at 30 fps, 20 fps after 20 s with no input, 10 fps while the veil is up, 2 fps with reduced motion, and 0 while a reader, map or travel covers the scene or the page-view fallback is active. The 30 fps cap is the ladder's last step.
drivers.when: at rest, which is where a visitor spends most of the time
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same idle rates on every tier. Only the last ladder step caps moving frames at 30 fps.
drivers.costGuess: Rest-state GPU load is 20 to 30 full frames per second, the same cost per frame as flight (about 50 to 100% of flight load at 30 vs 60 fps), so a phone or laptop on battery stays hot and throttles at a stop, which then hurts the next flight. Estimated from the loop logic.

drivers.what: Shader compile and first-use stalls: there is a warm-up. World.warm uploads each texture one frame at a time (deferred while flying), then gl.compileAsync on every scene root against a stand-in half-float 1x1 target (matching the composer's program key). three's compileAsync uses KHR_parallel_shader_compile when present. WarmDecor compiles decoration and overlay the same way. NOT warmed: the composer's own programs (merged EffectPass, luminance, down/up samplers, Kawase, depth copy), compiled synchronously on its first render (hidden behind the loading veil at start) and again at every pipeline rebuild.
drivers.where: scene.tsx:835-903 (warm), 2039-2075 (WarmDecor), 1518-1546 (pipeline rebuild effect with deps quality.msaa, quality.bloom, cloudShadows, holdFocus)
drivers.when: once per area load; once per pipeline rebuild (any ladder step on msaa or bloom, in either direction)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Climbs that rebuild the pipeline wait for the camera to rest (runtime.ts:313-316, scene.tsx:1992-1998). Steps DOWN do not wait: they rebuild mid-flight on a struggling device.
drivers.costGuess: A rebuild allocates new targets and compiles the merged effect shader synchronously: guess 30 to 150 ms hitch (the repo's own notes: 18 to 40 ms for a set's programs, 46 ms for decoration). Texture uploads 6 to 30 ms each at 4096 px (repo comment, scene.tsx:839).

drivers.what: Culling and sorting: three's own frustum culling per merged cell mesh (cell sizes above), no occlusion culling; opaque list sorted by material id then depth (three's painterSort), transparents far-to-near by object z; tree cards are alpha-tested or alpha-to-coverage (no early-Z on those); sky dome (64x32 sphere) is drawn last at the far plane so it shades only uncovered pixels. Static meshes have matrixAutoUpdate false, so updateMatrixWorld is a cheap walk. UncullOnce turns culling off for one frame behind the travel ink.
drivers.when: per frame (cheap)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on all tiers; ladder 'noCards' step hides tree card materials (scene.tsx:792-803).
drivers.costGuess: CPU side is small: a few hundred meshes, well under 1 ms. The heavy part is the triangle count, not sorting.

drivers.what: Canvas flags: frameloop demand, flat (no tone mapping), antialias only when post is off (Low), powerPreference high-performance, stencil false, alpha false, depth left at default true, preserveDrawingBuffer false (default), no logarithmicDepthBuffer. Camera near 0.5, far 9000. Shadows are off for the baked scene (shadows only if post && msaa && !baked).
drivers.when: fixed at context creation
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: antialias:true (native 4x canvas MSAA, cheap on tile GPUs; the card alpha-to-coverage relies on it, scene.tsx:1704-1707). Mid and High: antialias:false (the composer does MSAA on High; Mid has no anti-aliasing at all). Depth buffer is allocated on the canvas even when the composer draws to it with no depth test.
drivers.costGuess: Canvas depth on the post path is a wasted 4 B/px, about 8 MB at 1080p x1 or 19 MB at 4.67 Mpx, plus a clear. Small.

drivers.what: Low tier path: no composer, so the world draws straight to the (MSAA) canvas, then the overlay in a second gl.render. Missing compared with High: bloom, cloud shadow, sun haze, vignette, hue-preserving clip, dither, hold focus, reflections. Over-range glows are clipped per channel by the 8-bit canvas.
drivers.when: per frame
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low tier only (phones, software renderers, small devices).
drivers.costGuess: Cheapest path: roughly world pass + overlay, no full-screen post draws. Low's gap to High is mostly look, not cost.

mapNotes.area: Materials and per-pixel shader cost (materials.ts, glsl.ts fog, detail.ts, card-shading.ts, look.ts grade, range-look.ts, waterfall.ts wet rock, water.ts, reflect/*)
mapNotes.notes: Method: read the source only. No GPU timings, no profiles, nothing run. Every fetch and ALU number comes from counting GLSL operations as written; treat them as relative sizes, not milliseconds. The GLB files here are LFS pointers, so I could not count how many pixels use glaze/metal/iron or how large the triangles are; the manifest's tris and texBytes were read. The tier picture today: Low drops the rock and ground detail (detailWanted), has no post pass, uses analytic water and no cube probe, has 2 wet falls and no wet sheen; everything else (fog, grade, range look, surface reflections, cloud sea, sky, puffs, sheets, cards) is the same shader as High. Mid and High differ only in the far-rock octave count, wet-fall count, MSAA, the reflection resolution (1/3 vs 1/2, 256 vs 512 px, stand-ins vs full) and overlay tiering. Cheapest wins that cost nothing visible and help every tier: alpha test before grade on cards, detail/layers branches, cloud sea after opaque, puff/mist fog per vertex, reflection pass with detail off, hold-still reflection reuse. The three biggest per-pixel changes with real engineering are the fog LUT, the baked sky environment, and the range-weight lookup. Features switched by #define: none inside a program; program variants are made by patching source and the cache key (materials.ts:733-735), so tier-dropped detail really is a smaller program; the rest are uniforms. Precision: no mediump anywhere, so all highp. I did not look at grass.tsx, flames.tsx, post/ or texture formats, which other areas cover. Two things worth confirming on a real device with ?debug=1: how many ms the pond pass and the six cube faces cost (window.__sectReflect, SpanTimer in reflect/timer.ts), and the real share of sky, cloud sea and rock pixels per stop.

drivers.what: Fog chunk runs on every fogged pixel of every baked material: cloud depth, haze depth (two spans), aerial colour. About 10-12 exp/pow calls plus ~60 ALU. Applies to rock, ground, buildings, cards, pond, waterfall sheets. All of it is recomputed per pixel from (camera y, ray y, distance).
drivers.when: per pixel, per frame, every tier
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier. SECT_MIST is a #define (off at the defaults), so mist costs 2 more exp only where the look enables it.
drivers.costGuess: ~70 ALU + ~12 SFU per pixel (SFU = special-function unit: exp, pow, log, sin, run at a quarter rate). Estimated by counting GLSL ops, not profiled. Roughly a third of a plain building pixel.

drivers.what: Low tier fog path also decodes and re-encodes sRGB per pixel, because three has already encoded the colour (colorspace_fragment) before fog_fragment. Per pixel: 3 pow to decode the colour, 3 pow to decode fogColor (a uniform, recomputed per pixel), 3 pow to encode, plus a 2-hash dither.
drivers.when: per pixel, Low tier only (no post pass)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Only Low pays it (the branch is a compile-time constant); High and Mid skip it
drivers.costGuess: ~9 pow = ~18 SFU extra per fogged pixel, more than the fog maths itself. Counted from GLSL.

drivers.what: The grade (sectGrade/sectGradeWith) on every baked texel: exposure, green tame, pow for contrast, shadow/highlight tint, saturation, exp shoulder. It is a pure function of the texel colour (plus range weights on rock/ground/foliage). Range materials call sectGradeWith with mixed parameters, so the tint mixes are per pixel too.
drivers.where: client/src/lib/sect/look.ts:616-651; injected at materials.ts:779-809; range variants range-look.ts:612-643
drivers.when: per pixel
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on all tiers
drivers.costGuess: ~45-55 ALU + ~6 SFU per pixel (one pow, a 3-channel exp, 3 smoothsteps). About 30 percent of a plain building pixel.

drivers.what: Rock detail stack (high and mid): photo detail with three world projections x two layers = 6 fetches of tSectDetail, 3 pow for the projection weights, ground tint (2 fetches), clump (2 fetches), far-rock 3D noise (1 fetch per octave, 2 on high, 1 on mid), rock streak noise (1 fetch), mossy-rock gate computed a second time. Everything runs even where its fade is 0, because the code is branch-free. Photo detail fades out at 150 m and far rock at 700 m, but most range cliffs are 150-1500 m away.
drivers.where: client/src/lib/sect/detail.ts:762-776 (sectDetail), 806-814 and 828-843 (apply), 535-558, 564-587; fade constants detail.ts:75, 223-231; no-branch note at detail.ts:781-784
drivers.when: per pixel of every rock material
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: not patched at all (detailWanted false, detail.ts:461-465). Mid: one far-rock octave (rockFarOctaves, detail.ts:468). High: two octaves. The detail texture has anisotropy 8 (assets.ts:925).
drivers.costGuess: 13-14 fetches + ~250-300 ALU on high rock (5-6 fewer ALU on mid), on top of ~300 ALU base. Counted from GLSL. Wasted beyond 150 m, i.e. most rock pixels in wide shots.

drivers.what: Ground (lawn) detail stack: 2 detail fetches, ground tint 2, clump 2, wind sheen 1, far-lawn lump 1 = 8 fetches + hue rotation (cos, sin) and two clump layers. Same no-branch design: sheen fades at 320 m, clumps at 260 m, photo detail at 140 m, but all fetches always run.
drivers.when: per pixel of every ground material
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: none of it (not patched). Mid and High: identical. Lawns carry the range, so most pixels are far.
drivers.costGuess: 9 fetches (with the atlas) + ~180 ALU above the Low base of ~260 ALU. Counted from GLSL.

drivers.what: sectRangeW: a 16-slot loop over uSectAreas for every rock, ground and foliage pixel (breaks at the first empty slot, so ~11 iterations), then sectBuilt (one fetch, rock only). It is a smooth function of world position (25 m fade) recomputed per pixel.
drivers.where: client/src/lib/sect/range-look.ts:524-551; used at materials.ts:788; RANGE_MAX_AREAS = 16 (range-look.ts:30); built grid cell 2.5 m (range-look.ts:160)
drivers.when: per pixel of rock, ground, near trees and tree cards, all tiers (surfaceClass is read from userData, not from the tier, materials.ts:729-732)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier, including Low (Low rock/ground still compile the range grade even though the detail is dropped)
drivers.costGuess: ~90 ALU per pixel (11 iterations of a few ops, sqrt+smoothstep only inside a radius), +1 fetch on rock. Counted from GLSL.

drivers.what: Tree cards run the whole shade before the alpha test. In three's fragment order the grade/foliage/canopy block (injected after color_fragment) comes before alphamap/alphatest, so every fragment that is about to be discarded still pays for the foliage grade, tree shade, foliage range (sqrt, saturation cap, bark gate), canopy variation (2 value-noise = 8 sin) and the range loop. Sprite cards also take 2 derivative terms for mip boost and a cross/normalize for the view fade.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/materials.ts:779-809 (grade) vs 936-948 (card patch replaces alphamap/alphatest later); card-shading.ts:135-171, 178-201, 209-229, 236-248; range-look.ts:557-605
drivers.when: per card fragment, including transparent texels. Crossed quads + a top quad per tree, so overdraw is 2-3x in canopy.
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same shader on all tiers. Differences: alpha to coverage when msaa > 0 or on Low's canvas (sect-experience.tsx:532, materials.ts:955-958 alphaTest 0.4 vs 0.42), and the last rung of the quality ladder turns cards off.
drivers.costGuess: ~450 ALU + ~25 SFU + 1-2 fetches per card fragment; roughly 40-60 percent of the cut-out card is transparent, so ~35-50 percent of that ALU is thrown away. Estimated by counting; the fraction is a guess for needle/sprite alpha. `discard` also costs early-Z / hidden-surface removal on tile-based GPUs.

drivers.what: Metal, glaze, iron and Heart-Mirror surfaces call sectEnvSky per pixel: 1 sky fetch + atan + asin + two normalize + ~9 sin for the far-ridge and near-pillar silhouettes (these depend only on azimuth) + pow(sunSide,4) + the haze mix (4 exp) + sectEnvSun (2 pow with big exponents). Also dFdx/dFdy face normal, reflect, Schlick pow5.
drivers.when: per pixel of every tagged surface (roof glaze, metal trim, black iron), all tiers
drivers.tierBehaviour: Identical on every tier; Low gets no cheaper variant. (The Heart-Mirror cube path adds 2 cube fetches on High and Mid only, materials.ts:405-425.)
drivers.costGuess: ~250-300 ALU-equivalents per tagged pixel (about 20 SFU). Share of screen unknown: GLBs here are LFS pointers, so I could not count tagged materials.

drivers.what: Pond shader. Planar path (High, Mid, while a reflection was rendered): per pixel of the area's atlas material it does dFdx/dFdy normal, plane and bounds tests; on open-water pixels it adds 4 cos ripples, reflect, Schlick, 4 half-float bilinear taps. Analytic path (Low, or any frame without a planar image): sectEnvSky plus, where the reflected ray hits the mirror disc, the full procedural Heart-Mirror (arm, runes with atan, cradle loop over lathe slices, rim, up to ~8 composited layers each calling sectMirrorShade with more sectEnvSky). Both paths are compiled into one program.
drivers.when: per pixel of the pond area's water material (shared atlas, so the test runs well beyond the pond); heavy part only on water pixels, mirror part only where the ray meets the disc
drivers.tierBehaviour: Planar on High (0.5 texel/pixel) and Mid (1/3); analytic on Low and as the fallback elsewhere. uHasReflect is a uniform, so both branches live in the same program (register pressure on every tier).
drivers.costGuess: Planar: ~4 fetches + ~80 ALU on water pixels. Analytic with mirror: ~500-900 ALU-equivalents on mirror-hit pixels (counted: 8 layers x shade + cradle loop). Low only pays it at the Heart-Mirror stop.

drivers.what: Pond planar reflection pass: a second full scene render per frame while the open water is on screen and within 320 m, not 'lean'. It draws the global backdrop (~1.48M tris) and the mirror's own area in full (~1.06M tris), other drawn areas as stand-ins, no grass, into a half-float target the size of the drawing buffer x scale (only the pond rectangle is filled). Every frame, even when the camera is still.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/reflect/index.ts:129-160, 229-247; reflect/pond.ts:53-147; reflect/plan.ts:13-39 (scale high 0.5, mid 1/3, maxDistance 320, view standIns true); manifest.json globalTris 1476322, mirror tris 1063102
drivers.when: per frame while the pond is on screen within 320 m
drivers.tierBehaviour: High: 0.5 scale, Mid: 1/3, Low: none (analytic). Skipped when the ladder is at 'lean'. Whole-mesh frustum culling only, so the narrowed frustum rarely drops a chunk.
drivers.costGuess: Vertex side ~2.5M tris extra per frame (my count from the manifest; culling may cut it). Fragment side: High 1080p at 1.5x DPR = 2880x1620 x 0.25 = 1.17 MP at most; Mid 1080p x 1/9 = 0.23 MP. Memory: High ~9 MB colour (RGBA16F) + ~5 MB depth, Mid ~2 MB + ~1 MB. Estimated from sizes, not measured.

drivers.what: Heart-Mirror cube probe: six faces rendered one per frame. High: 512 px faces, everything drawn at full detail (all drawn areas, grass on); Mid: 256 px faces, stand-ins, no grass. First capture within 250 m, then a fresh capture every 6 s while the mirror is on screen within 160 m, and at once when the drawn sets or quality step change.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/reflect/index.ts:116-130, 146-153; reflect/probe.ts:25-62; reflect/plan.ts:43-58 (size, view, maxDistance 250, refreshDistance 160, refreshSeconds 6), 97-145
drivers.when: 6 frames every 6 s at the mirror stop; mipmap build on the last face
drivers.tierBehaviour: High: full detail 512 px; Mid: stand-ins 256 px; Low: none
drivers.costGuess: High: each face is a vertex-heavy pass with up to 4 full areas + backdrop = ~6-8M tris before culling (estimated: ~1.0-1.7M per chunk in manifest.json), small pixel count (0.26 MP). Likely a visible hitch for 6 frames every 6 s on High. Memory: cube 512x512x6 x 8 B x 1.33 (mips) = ~17 MB + 6 depth buffers ~6 MB; Mid ~6 MB total.

drivers.what: Reflection passes run the full main-view shaders (rock/ground detail layers, wet rock, range look, clumps) at half or third resolution, through a rippled, blurred reflection. Only the soft-depth read is switched off (SOFT_DEPTH.uHasDepth = 0).
drivers.when: every reflection pass
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same shaders as the main pass
drivers.costGuess: The pond and cube passes cost fragment work the viewer cannot see: ~13 fetches on rock, ~8 on lawn per reflected pixel.

drivers.what: Wet rock loop in every baked material that is not a card or glow: loops up to uWetCount (<= 6) falls, ~6 ops per iteration for the y-test, ~40 more inside a fall's band, plus a drip noise fetch and pow(.,24) on wet pixels. uWetSheen is 0 on Low but the spec and fresnel pow still run.
drivers.where: client/src/lib/sect/waterfall.ts:665-742 (WET.perTier high 6 / mid 4 / low 2 at 433-436); patched at materials.ts:722, 808; counts set via assets.ts:901
drivers.when: per pixel while falls are selected (uWetCount > 0); 0 cost when the count is 0
drivers.tierBehaviour: Count scales by tier (6/4/2). Same code. Uniform branch, so no cost with count 0.
drivers.costGuess: ~5 ALU when count 0; ~25-45 ALU with 2-6 falls near the camera (mostly early `continue`); +~60 ALU and 1 fetch on wet pixels. Counted from GLSL.

drivers.what: Cloud sea: 9 tNoise fetches per pixel (billow() x 3: height, +45 m lit step, +260 m shadow step; 3 octaves each) plus haze. Drawn FIRST among opaque (renderOrder -800, writes depth), so every pixel it covers is shaded and then painted over by islands and terrain.
drivers.when: per pixel below the horizon, every frame
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on all tiers. Relief fades at 1800-6500 m but the fetches still run.
drivers.costGuess: 9 fetches + ~120 ALU per covered pixel (counted). The sky dome already moved after the opaque pass for exactly this overdraw reason (scene.tsx:429-440, 'drawn first it shaded every pixel'; they measured 13 percent of the world pass on average and 24 percent at the gate), so the sea likely wastes a similar share.

drivers.what: Sky dome clouds: per sky pixel above the horizon, 2 layers x 2 samples (n and a sun-shifted nl for lighting) x 4 octaves = 16 tNoise fetches + the sky image fetch, plus atan/asin and fog maths. Already drawn after the opaque pass, only where nothing covers it.
drivers.when: per uncovered sky pixel, every frame; and again inside every reflection pass
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on all tiers
drivers.costGuess: 17 fetches + ~150 ALU per sky pixel (counted). Sky is perhaps 30-50 percent of the frame in upward views (my guess from the flight).

drivers.what: Cloud puffs: up to ~1000 camera-facing instanced sprites (clouds.json has 1021, packPuffs keeps those within 2600 m of the path), alpha blended, depthWrite off, sorted far to near. Fragment: 2 noise fetches + 1 depth fetch (composer depth, High and Mid only), sphere lighting, then haze depth, haze colour and cloud depth, each with several exp. That fog uses vF and vDist, which are per-instance constants (not per pixel).
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/materials.ts:1796-1913 (fog at 1904-1907; vF/vDist set at 1846-1850); scene.tsx:598-629; clouds.ts:40-57
drivers.when: per sprite fragment; overdraw is high where banks overlap
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same shader on all tiers (no depth fetch on Low because there is no composer depth)
drivers.costGuess: ~3 fetches + ~160 ALU + ~8 SFU per fragment, of which the redundant per-fragment fog is ~60 ALU + ~8 SFU. Overdraw depth unknown (guess 3-8 layers in a bank).

drivers.what: Waterfall sheets: 5 texture fetches per fragment (clump, streak, strand, two 'soft' far-field), all always fetched, even though the near patterns are mixed away past 130-260 m, then ~40 smoothsteps. Transparent, DoubleSide, three layers per fall (core, curtain, veil by vertex colour).
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/materials.ts:1618-1650 (fetches 1618-1629; far mix 1631-1635), 1553-1559 (DoubleSide, transparent); waterfall.ts SHEET.farFrom 130, farTo 260 (line 150-151)
drivers.when: per sheet fragment, overdraw 2-4x on large falls
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same material on all tiers; only spray and puff counts change by tier (waterfall-fx.tsx:677-684)
drivers.costGuess: 5 fetches + ~150 ALU per fragment (counted).

drivers.what: Anisotropic filtering of 8 on every baked texture on every tier, including Low (set in one place, before first upload).
drivers.when: every atlas fetch (the one fetch every material makes); detail fetches on high/mid
drivers.tierBehaviour: Not tiered: Low gets the same 8x
drivers.costGuess: Up to 8 bilinear taps (x2 for trilinear) per fetch on grazing surfaces such as lawns and terraces. Real bandwidth cost on integrated and mobile GPUs. Not measured.

drivers.what: Precision and features-by-define vs uniform. No precision statements anywhere (grep found none outside comments), so every shader is the renderer's default, highp. Variants are made by patching source and the program cache key (detail kind, water, surface class, range class, wet, tree, shade), so tiers that drop detail get a genuinely different, smaller program. Within a program the tier switches are uniforms: uSectRockOctaves, uSectRockFar, uSectGroundLayers, uSectDetailOn, uWetCount, uHasReflect, uSectMirrorEnvOn, uStreaks, uDetail.
drivers.when: compile time vs per pixel
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: smaller program for rock/ground (no detail), but none for fog, grade, range, surfaces, water, sky, sea, puffs, sheets. A uniform branch skips the work (cheap), but a uniform that only multiplies (uSectDetailOn, uSectGroundLayers, uSectRockFar, uWetSheen) leaves the fetches and maths in place.
drivers.costGuess: Qualitative. mediump (fp16) would give up to ~1.3-1.6x ALU on Mali/Adreno for colour math, none on Apple/desktop; world positions and fog integrals must stay highp.

mapNotes.area: Live effects and main-thread CPU work per frame (grass, flames, waterfall fx, life, petals/cranes, cloud puffs, hotspot picking, render driver, music, overlay CSS, ink travel, map)
mapNotes.notes:
Read-only research; nothing was run or profiled, so every millisecond above is an estimate from code structure (loop counts, instance counts, draw counts), not a measurement. GLB files are LFS pointers here, so triangle numbers come from manifest.json, clouds.json (1021 puffs; 260 are mist), meta.json (6 fires, 5 waterfalls, 103 hotspots, 11 areas) and camera.json (1729 frames, 2580 m, about 1.5 m per authored frame). To check any estimate with the debug hooks on a real device (?debug=1): window.__sect.grass.stats() gives cpuMs (grass pass) and areas[id].buildMs/longestMs; window.__sect.stats.ladder() gives frame and GPU times; window.__sectReflect.gpu() gives the reflection passes' GPU time; window.__sect.info() gives draw calls and triangles; window.__sectFlames[chunk].show toggles each fire draw.

Draw calls added by live effects (at most): grass 96 (High) / 28 (Mid) / 0 (Low); flames up to 4 per fire chunk (Low has no light draw); waterfall fx 3; life 3 (butterflies hidden on Low); petals, cranes, forge fire, formation core, incense, cloud puffs 1 each. So about 25 non-grass draws at High and about 20 at Low.

Still fully on at Low: cloud puffs (761), petals (half), cranes, flames (thinned, all fires on), waterfall skirt/spray/mist (thinned), birds and motes (35%), forge fire, incense, formation core, idle motion, hover picking, ink travel and music. Off at Low: grass, mist puffs, butterflies, blaze light, reflections, postprocessing.

Allocation per frame: the only large source is the cloud-puff subarray views (about 100-150 KB per moving frame). Smaller ones: CameraRig (sampleCamera object spread, framedHolds arrays three times, composeLook arrays), Driver's `counts` template string, cranes (about 15 objects), the Hotspots `pointed` closure, the Reflections signature string, and each pick's Map/arrays. I expect these to cost minor GC but nothing visible.

Worker candidates, in order of value: grass build (pure typed-array maths); cloud-puff sort (not needed if the incremental sort lands); buildLifeTables and packPuffs at mount (one-off, hidden behind the loading veil, low value; packPuffs is about 1021 x 288 hypot calls at mount, scene.tsx:601-612, and could be precomputed into clouds.json offline). Precompute candidates: the kept-puff list and density scale, the life tables.

Web Audio verdict: cheap on weak phones in CPU terms; the cost is RAM (about 38 MB per decoded track, two kept on phones). decodeAudioData happens off the main thread, but expect a short memory spike while an MP3 is decoded and the PCM is created.

Does not need changing: React state in the frame loop (none), the useFrame count (about 32, each trivial), idle motion, flames CPU, waterfall CPU, map view. The two best 'free for every tier' fixes are the cloud-puff sort and the render-rate classes (pointer/pulse and idle). The two that make Low/Mid closer to High at the same cost are grass-lite on Low and keeping the pond reflection cached at rest. I did not read the Post/composer, material shaders or the asset loader (other areas); two of my items (cloud overdraw, pond reflection cost) touch them, so check against that research to avoid double-counting.

drivers.what: Cloud puffs are re-sorted and re-uploaded on almost every moving frame. A comparator sort of about 1021 puffs (nearly 10k comparator calls), then 1021 `packed.subarray()` views created and copied, then a whole-buffer upload (about 53 KB). It re-runs whenever the camera has moved 0.5 m, and scrolling moves it several metres per display frame.
drivers.when: every moving frame (skipped at rest)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier. Only difference: Low drops the 260 `mist.*` puffs (scene.tsx:2327), so about 761 puffs instead of 1021. All puffs are always submitted: frustumCulled is false and instanceCount is fixed (scene.tsx:625-629).
drivers.costGuess: My estimate, not measured: about 0.2-0.5 ms of CPU on a desktop, 1-2 ms on a weak phone (typed-array sort with a JS comparator is slow in V8). The subarray views are about 100-150 KB of garbage per frame, roughly 6-9 MB/s at 60 fps. Draw count: 1. GPU side: about 1000 large soft sprites with 2 texture reads and 2 haze exp() each; overdraw not measured.

drivers.what: Grass per-frame cell pass and draw submission. Every built cell of every drawn area gets cellDistance (hypot), cellCount (binary search or ring lookup) and a frustum-sphere test. Survivors are sorted by distance with a comparator, fitBudget runs up to 4 iterations (each allocates a forEach closure), then instanceCount is set. The pass repeats at the 30 fps idle rate with identical results.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/grass.tsx:976-1054; tiers at client/src/lib/sect/grass.ts:134-137, grassTier at grass.ts:220-226
drivers.when: every rendered frame, including idle frames
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: off (no postprocessing). Mid: maxDraws 28, maxTufts 16,000, reach 110 m, share 0.4, which is about 144k triangles. High: 96 draws, 60,000 tufts, reach 300 m, about 540k triangles. A High device that has stepped down the ladder uses the mid grass.
drivers.costGuess: Estimate: the CPU pass is about 0.1-0.4 ms on a desktop, assuming 300-1000 cells in drawn areas (window.__sect.grass.stats().cpuMs reports the real figure). Submitting 96 instanced draws is about 1-3 ms of three.js CPU on a phone-class CPU (10-30 µs per draw); 28 draws about 0.3-0.8 ms. The code's own comment gives 0.15-0.25 ms GPU for High on an RTX 5080. Resident memory is 48 B per tuft (pos 12, colour 4, a 16, b 16).

drivers.what: Grass build per area, on the main thread. It reads every ground and rock triangle into JS arrays, scatters candidates, finds edges, makes fringe and rim bushes, reads roots back from the atlas, then makes cells and geometries. It runs in 6 ms slices separated by setTimeout(0), and is not gated on the camera being still or on idle time (the BVH builder is gated). It is pure typed-array math apart from the atlas readback.
drivers.when: once per area when its chunk loads (desktop: up to 5 resident areas)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Not built on Low. Mid and High build the same way, with the tier's own reach and density at build time.
drivers.costGuess: Unknown; read stats().areas[id].buildMs and longestMs on a real phone. By structure: 6 ms of work per 4-5 ms of timer gap is about 55-60% main-thread occupancy while a build runs, so a slice can land inside a frame. The ladder's 2 s settle window covers 'set ready' and 'first drawn', not the grass build, so slices could count as slow frames.

drivers.what: Idle render loop. At rest the full pipeline (world, overlay, composer on Mid/High) renders at 30 fps forever, dropping to 20 fps after 20 s with no input. Petals always move, so something is always changing. The rate is the same constant for every tier.
drivers.when: continuously while the tab is visible and no reader or map is open
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier. Only the ladder's last step (30 fps cap) or reduced motion (2 fps) changes it. A reader or the map stops it entirely (store.modal).
drivers.costGuess: Cost is 30 x frame cost. If a Mid frame is 8 ms of GPU, that is about 24% GPU duty and heat/battery drain while nobody touches the page. Not measured.

drivers.what: Hover pulse and pointer wake render at the full display rate. `pulse` (a hovered, focused or selected hotspot) and every pointermove (`wake(store, 200)`) put the Driver in 'always' mode with no cap. The cap (maxFps) is 0 on every tier and only the ladder's last step sets 30. The ladder only reacts to frames over about 20 ms, so a 90/120/144 Hz screen renders every display frame as long as the GPU keeps up.
drivers.when: while the mouse moves or a hotspot is hovered (desktop), and during any camera motion on high-refresh screens
drivers.tierBehaviour: No difference between tiers. A 120 Hz phone on Low or Mid has no 60 fps ceiling.
drivers.costGuess: A hover glow is a 0.5 Hz sine and the label is placed by a pick that is already throttled to 50 ms, so rendering it at 120 fps buys nothing. A GPU that could do 70-100 fps on a 120 Hz screen runs flat out; I estimate 33-60% of the GPU/battery for the same picture at 60 fps.

drivers.what: Hotspot picking and hover label. Picking: runs when the pointer moved (at most every 50 ms) AND every 0.25 s while the pointer is anywhere inside the canvas, even when nothing changed. Each pick allocates a Map, arrays and `[...pk.meshes]` copies, tests all pick boxes, raycasts BVH meshes, and `occluded()` walks every occluder mesh (bounding sphere applyMatrix4 each) plus BVH rays. Label: while a hotspot is hovered and the camera moves, onHover runs every frame and calls getBoundingClientRect on every visible panel plus offsetWidth/offsetHeight right after style writes, which forces a layout each frame.
drivers.when: picks up to 20/s while moving the mouse, 4/s otherwise; the forced layout every frame while hovering and scrolling (desktop mouse only, a finger never hovers)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier. Touch devices skip the hover path (BVH is skipped on touch, background-work bvhWanted).
drivers.costGuess: Estimate: 0.2-1 ms per pick, assuming a few dozen occluder meshes; the forced style/layout flush is 0.1-0.5 ms per frame. Neither measured.

drivers.what: Separate requestAnimationFrame loops that run every display frame forever, besides the render Driver's own loop: the hold-panel tick (writes opacity/transform on up to 11 panels when u changes, allocates holdPresence arrays) and the portrait-turn tick, which also runs on desktop and does `store.map.holds.find(closure)` each frame. Together with the Driver, that is 3 rAF callbacks per display frame, even at rest.
drivers.when: every display frame (60-120 Hz) while the page is visible
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier.
drivers.costGuess: Under 20 µs per call, so under 0.1 ms per frame. The cost is keeping the main thread awake 180-360 times a second at rest on a phone (power), not frame time.

drivers.what: Number of useFrame callbacks. scene.tsx declares 22, of which 2 are DebugProbe (debug only) and 1 is PlainRender or Post, so about 19 in production (Reflections still registers 3 on Low even though they do nothing there). fx.tsx 5 (Petals, ForgeFire, FormationCore, IncenseSmoke, Cranes), life 1, grass 1, waterfall 1, flames 1 per resident chunk.
drivers.when: each rendered frame
drivers.tierBehaviour: About 32 on desktop (5 resident chunks), about 30 on phone/Low. Counts do not change with tier.
drivers.costGuess: Most are a few uniform writes. Together, excluding cloud sort, grass pass and picks, I estimate well under 0.5 ms a frame on a desktop. They are not the problem.

drivers.what: React state in the frame loop: essentially none. setAtHold and setActiveArea fire only on change; setHovered bails out on equal values; setLookedBack and setIntroUp run on a 150 ms interval with equal values (no re-render); travel progress is quantised to 2%. Panels and the hover label are moved with direct style writes.
drivers.when: on change only
drivers.tierBehaviour: n/a
drivers.costGuess: Negligible. No re-render of the canvas tree: SectCanvas is memoised (scene.tsx:2462).

drivers.what: Planar pond reflection and mirror cube capture. The pond reflection re-submits the loaded sets (mirror area at full detail, others as stand-ins) into a 1/2 (High) or 1/3 (Mid) resolution target on every rendered frame while the pond is on screen and within 320 m, even at rest. The cube capture is amortised: one face a frame, then every 6 s. Also allocates a `signature` string each frame while near the mirror.
drivers.when: each rendered frame at the Still Pond stop and its approach
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low: nothing (Reflections still registers its callbacks). Mid: pond at 1/3, cube 256 px, grass off, stand-ins. High: pond at 1/2, cube 512 px, grass on for the cube.
drivers.costGuess: Estimate: re-submits the mirror chunk's draws (a chunk is about 1.0-1.5M triangles by the manifest) at about 1/4-1/9 of the pixels; I'd guess 1-3 ms GPU and a similar draw-submission CPU on Mid-class hardware at those stops. Not measured; another area may be covering this.

drivers.what: Flames. One useFrame per resident chunk. Each tests every fire against the frustum, sets a few uniforms and recolours the molten-glow materials (`color.copy(base).multiplyScalar`) even for undrawn chunks. Draws per chunk with fires: up to 4 (blaze light, furnace mouths, flame cards, embers). Cards: cauldron 6/5/3, kiln 2/2/1 each, blaze 6/5/4 each. Embers: mouth 18/12/6, kiln 24/16/8, blaze sparks 16/10/5 (+1 glow).
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/flames.tsx:967-1031, client/src/lib/sect/flames.ts:165-169 (flameTier); meta.json has 6 fires (3 furnace mouths, 2 chimney kilns, 1 cauldron) plus carved blazes
drivers.when: every frame; draws only while a fire is in view and its chunk drawn
drivers.tierBehaviour: Every fire stays on at Low, just thinner: fewer cards, 1 sheet instead of 2, fewer embers, no blaze light. High/Mid differ mostly in embers.
drivers.costGuess: CPU is tens of microseconds. GPU: the furnace-mouth fragment shader ray-traces a fire box per pixel; it is only a few quads but can fill a big part of the screen at the forge stop. Not measured.

drivers.what: Waterfall foot effects. Three draws while a grounded fall is in view and its chunk drawn: foam skirt (one mesh), spray (instanced streaks, 250/160/80 by tier), mist puffs (4 slots x 10 instances always submitted, the shader trims to 10/8/6 per foot). The CPU only sets uniforms and loops at most 8 feet.
drivers.when: each frame while a foot is in view
drivers.tierBehaviour: Counts thin by tier; all three draws stay on at Low.
drivers.costGuess: CPU negligible. GPU fill-rate for large soft mist sprites with a 2-frame flipbook blend. Not measured.

drivers.what: Life (birds, motes, butterflies). Three instanced draws whose motion is entirely in the vertex shaders; the CPU does a frustum test per group and sets 3 uniforms each. buildLifeTables runs synchronously inside useMemo at mount.
drivers.when: per frame uniform writes; tables once at mount
drivers.tierBehaviour: Instances are the first N of each rank-ordered table: 100% / 60% / 35%; butterflies are off on Low. Birds, motes and petals stay on at Low.
drivers.costGuess: By my reading of the LIFE constants (70 motes per hold x 11, 28 per blossom, 20 per pond, 30 relic, qi at falls; 3 flocks of 5-20 birds per hold) it is on the order of 1-2k motes and a few hundred birds at High, all drawn with additive blending. Table build is one-off, not measured. Per-frame CPU is negligible.

drivers.what: Petals, cranes, incense, forge fire, formation core. Petals (520 on Mid/High, 260 on Low) and the others are shader-driven and cost one uniform write each. Cranes are the exception: 5 cranes updated on the CPU every frame with 3 DynamicDraw buffer uploads, and cranePose allocates two arrays plus an object per crane per frame, plus a forEach closure.
drivers.when: each frame
drivers.tierBehaviour: Petals halve on Low; the rest are the same on every tier.
drivers.costGuess: Cranes: about 15 allocations and 3 tiny uploads per frame, microseconds. Cleanliness more than cost. Everything else: draw count 1 each.

drivers.what: Web Audio music. Two things matter: decoded memory and a 100 ms control loop. Each decoded 48 kHz stereo float track is about 38 MB on average (25-52 MB; computed from the durations in public/sect/audio/music.json). Phones and deviceMemory <= 4 keep 2 decoded tracks, desktops 3. The control tick (every 100 ms) runs apply(), which builds several spread arrays and Sets each time. Audio-thread work is 1-2 looping buffer sources plus 3 gain nodes, with latencyHint 'playback' at the file rate (48 kHz), which is negligible.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/experience/music-engine.ts:236-330 (apply), music.tsx:221-240 (100 ms tick), 59-80 (AudioContext options); client/src/lib/sect/music.ts:358-376 (keepPlan, musicBudget)
drivers.when: memory is held while sound has been turned on; tick every 100 ms
drivers.tierBehaviour: Not tied to the quality tier. Tied to coarse pointer and deviceMemory only. Nothing downloads before the first gesture with sound on.
drivers.costGuess: About 76 MB of decoded audio on a phone, about 115 MB on a desktop. CPU is not the issue: decodeAudioData runs off the main thread, the steady mix is about 1-2% of a core, and the 100 ms tick is tens of microseconds plus about 10 small allocations.

drivers.what: CSS backdrop-filter over the live canvas. `.sect-panel` has blur(10px) saturate(1.1) at 58% alpha. `.sect-plate` has blur(8px) at 82% alpha and is on at least 15 persistent or hover UI elements (labels, chips, the menu/sound/map buttons, the hint, the hover label, lore card, tooltips). The canvas behind them changes every rendered frame, so the browser's compositor re-captures and re-blurs each one every frame. A panel mid-fade (opacity < 1) also needs an offscreen group.
drivers.where: client/src/app/sect/sect.css:327-335 (.sect-panel), 375-380 (.sect-plate), 783-794 (orb tooltip), 1318-1337 (.sect-map, blur 3px); element list: overlay.tsx:41,46,131,205,242,295,325,339,371,481,533,561, sound-toggle.tsx:230,277, lore-card.tsx:42
drivers.when: every composited frame while the element is visible
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier; no coarse-pointer or Low switch exists (sect.css has @media only for reduced-motion and sizes).
drivers.costGuess: Estimate: 6-10 small backdrop passes per frame plus one large hold panel; on a tile-based mobile GPU I'd guess 0.3-1.5 ms of compositor GPU per frame, unmeasured (check Chrome trace 'Composite' and 'Raster' with the page flying). The map's full-screen blur(3px) is over a canvas that has stopped redrawing, so it is cheap.

drivers.what: Ink travel and map. The map is DOM/SVG only and the 3D loop stops under it, so nothing runs per frame there. InkTravel builds 3 blot sprites at every travel start on the main thread: 256 px canvases with `filter: blur(1.5px)` and 9 filled 120-point shapes each. Then a half-resolution 2D canvas is redrawn every frame (full fillRect plus radial gradient plus 5 drawImage). At dpr >= 2 the canvas is full CSS resolution (k = 0.5 x dpr clamped 1..2).
drivers.when: once per fast-travel, for about 1-2 s
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier; reduced motion uses a plain opacity fade.
drivers.costGuess: Estimate: sprite creation 5-30 ms on a weak phone, landing at the start of the travel; per-frame 2D work is small on a GPU-accelerated canvas, about 1.3M px at 1440x900 and dpr 2. One-off, not per frame.

drivers.what: Idle motion (idle.ts). updateIdle recolours a handful of glow materials and re-places a few rigid pieces (forge artifacts, formation core, library scrolls, cranes) for each drawn chunk; tree/banner sway is in the vertex shader on a shared clock.
drivers.when: each frame per drawn chunk (skipped under reduced motion once rested)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier.
drivers.costGuess: A few dozen matrix multiplies and colour writes: tens of microseconds. Not a concern.

mapNotes.area: Assets, GPU memory, loading and the page around the canvas
mapNotes.notes: What I could not verify. (1) GLB files here are LFS pointers, so I never saw per-file texture counts, pixel sizes or the merged-vs-chunk geometry split. Texture facts come from manifest.json (fileTexBytes shows each full area has 1-2 atlases of 4096x4096 plus its trees texture; low copies are 2048). (2) The bundle numbers are from the main checkout's .next folder (built Oct 25), not rebuilt here, so treat them as close, not exact. (3) All GPU and compositor cost guesses are arithmetic or the owner's own comments in the code, not profiles. I did not run anything. (4) Where bitmaps live in RAM (CPU or GPU process) depends on the browser. (5) Vercel's default Cache-Control for public/ files is from memory; confirm with curl -I. (6) Three's bundled basis transcoder version in r186 was not checked for newer formats (XUASTC); ask before assuming 6x6 ASTC is available. What the code already does well and I did not propose changing: workers for gunzip, meshopt and BVH, 5 ms prepare slices, one texture per frame, bitmap close after upload, UV/colour array release, deferred uploads while moving, the demand frameloop with a 30/20/10 fps idle rate, and pausing the scene under the map and readers (so the map blur and reader blurs cost little once open). The single biggest lever is GPU texture memory (about 1.2 GB on the full window); the single biggest download item is geometry, not textures, so KTX2 trades download for memory and should be tested on one area first. Owner-rule fit: the CSS blur removal, preload, caching, JIT decode, lazy BVH and geometry warm-up are free on every tier; KTX2 and anisotropy are the only ideas that change how any tier looks, and KTX2 should look the same or better.

drivers.what: Texture memory on the GPU, High and roomy Medium desktops. Window is 2 areas each side plus 1 spare, so up to 6 areas of 4096 px atlases (RGBA8, so 4 bytes per pixel, plus a third for mips) stay resident.
drivers.when: resident the whole visit, grows as the visitor scrolls
drivers.tierBehaviour: High and Medium with 8 GB+ (or 8+ cores) get this window. Nothing else changes between them.
drivers.costGuess: Worst 6 areas in a row (gate to library) sum to 1,224 MB from the manifest, plus 14.7 MB global = about 1.24 GB of textures. Geometry adds about 0.33 GB (10.8M triangles at about 31 bytes each, the figure streaming.ts:84-86 measured). Total about 1.6 GB. One extra area is kept during a handover, so the real peak is higher (about +250 MB).

drivers.what: Texture memory on the GPU, Medium desktop with less memory (narrow window: 1 each side + 1 spare). Still the 4096 px set.
drivers.when: resident the whole visit
drivers.tierBehaviour: Smaller window, same texture size
drivers.costGuess: Worst 4 areas (gate to arena) = 876 MB with global, plus about 0.2 GB geometry = about 1.1 GB. Computed from manifest texBytes.

drivers.what: Texture memory on the GPU, Low tier and touch Medium (2048 px set, 1 each side + 1 spare). Touch High keeps 4096 px but only the current area plus 1 spare.
drivers.where: streaming.ts:117-118; runtime.ts:199-205 (lowTextures true for Low, and for coarse-pointer Mid); sect_pack.py:108,1205-1207 (low copies)
drivers.when: resident the whole visit
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low set is 26-45% of the full texture bytes per area (manifest texBytesLow / texBytes)
drivers.costGuess: Worst 4 low areas (mission window) = 302 MB with global. Touch High worst 2 areas = 487 MB. streaming.ts:89-96 reports 0.6-0.8 GB total on a phone once geometry and script buffers are added.

drivers.what: Texture decode path. GLTFLoader uses ImageBitmapLoader on every current browser (only Safari under 17 and Firefox under 98 fall back to HTMLImageElement). Each embedded WebP is wrapped in a Blob and decoded with createImageBitmap, which runs off the main thread. parseAsync waits until ALL of a chunk's textures are decoded, so a whole chunk's bitmaps sit in RAM at once.
drivers.where: node_modules/three/examples/jsm/loaders/GLTFLoader.js:2654-2660, 3340-3420; assets.ts:476 (parseAsync); assets.ts:1183-1198 (main and _trees files parsed together)
drivers.when: once per area load; up to 2 area loads in flight (MAX_PARALLEL, streaming.ts:44)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same code on every tier. Low decodes the 2048 px copy, so a quarter of the pixels.
drivers.costGuess: Transient decoded RGBA per area = manifest texBytes minus the mip third, about 180-270 MB on full, 60-75 MB on low. Two loads overlapping could add about 0.4-0.5 GB of process memory on top of what is resident. I could not measure where Chrome keeps the bitmaps (CPU or GPU process); this is arithmetic.

drivers.what: Texture upload. One texture per animation frame via gl.initTexture, then the bitmap is closed (prepare.ts:323-333). Mipmaps are generated on the GPU at upload (GLTFLoader sets generateMipmaps for non-compressed textures, GLTFLoader.js:3323). Uploads wait while the camera moves fast, a jump is flying, or the view turns, but never longer than 500 ms per area.
drivers.where: scene.tsx:835-863 (warm, initTexture at 858, nextFrame at 862); background-work.ts:149-190 (deferUpload, UPLOAD_MAX_WAIT_MS 500)
drivers.when: once per texture when its area arrives
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same logic on every tier; Low just uploads 4x fewer pixels.
drivers.costGuess: 6-30 ms stall per 4096 atlas on desktop (the owner's own measurement in background-work.ts:5-6). A 2048 atlas is a quarter of the data, so roughly 1.5-8 ms (my scaling, not measured). A 4096 area has 2-3 big atlases plus tree textures, so 3-6+ frames of uploads.

drivers.what: Anisotropic filtering of 8x is forced on every baked texture of every set (min(8, GPU max)), on every tier. The detail texture asks for 8, strands 4, grass clump 4.
drivers.when: per pixel, every frame, wherever an atlas is seen at a slant (ground, roofs, walls)
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier: nothing reads the tier here.
drivers.costGuess: Up to 8x more texture taps per fragment at grazing angles, on top of trilinear. On a phone or integrated GPU that is texture bandwidth, but I cannot size it without a GPU profile.

drivers.what: Vertex memory. Chunk meshes stay as meshopt output (16-bit positions). Anything merged per spatial cell is rebuilt as plain Float32 for every attribute (position, uv, colour, uv1 on cards). That is about 32-40 bytes per vertex. Only uv, uv1 and colour CPU arrays are freed after upload; positions and indices stay on the CPU for BVH, grass and occlusion.
drivers.where: prepare.ts:149-167 (toFloat32), prepare.ts:179-233 (mergeSliced wants Float32, not normalized), prepare.ts:435-471 (releaseAfterGpuUpload)
drivers.when: per area load; resident while the area is
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier
drivers.costGuess: Geometry about 0.25-0.32 GB GPU on the full window and 0.17-0.22 GB on a phone, plus 0.16-0.29 GB of script buffers on a phone (streaming.ts:84-96, the owner's measurements). What share of that is merged geometry I could not tell without the GLBs (they are LFS pointers here).

drivers.what: Geometry upload is not warmed. warm() only uploads textures and compiles programs. Vertex buffers go up when three first renders each mesh, so the first frames after an area becomes drawable upload whatever is in the frustum.
drivers.when: first draw of each mesh in an area, in the frames right after it arrives
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier
drivers.costGuess: Per area about 30-45 MB of vertex data (1.0-2.1M triangles at about 31 bytes), a fraction of it in view at first. Plausibly a few ms to 10 ms of driver time in those frames. Unmeasured; check with ?debug=1 frame times at an area boundary.

drivers.what: Download size. Each area is 8.7-12.9 MB gzip (full) or 5.7-10.4 MB (low). Global backdrop is 9.6 MB and 1.48M triangles on every tier (no globalLow in the manifest). Whole flight is 111 MB full, 87.5 MB low, plus 9.6 MB global.
drivers.where: manifest.json bytes / bytesLow / globalBytes; sect_pack.py:666-667 (WebP q82 full, q88 proto), sect_pack.py:559-564 (gzip -9), sect_pack.py:1585 (globalLow only if the global files have a 2048 variant)
drivers.when: once per area, streamed ahead on desktop, at rest on phones
drivers.tierBehaviour: Low saves only 16-29% of the bytes (87.5 vs 111 MB total) while saving 65-75% of texture memory, because geometry dominates the download.
drivers.costGuess: From full-minus-low sizes (23.7 MB total, assuming 2048 WebP is about 45% of the 4096 bytes) textures are about 43 MB of the 111 MB, roughly 0.8 bits per pixel over 417 Mpx. So geometry is about 60% of the download (about 68 MB). This is an inference, not a measurement.

drivers.what: Main-thread work when an area arrives. gunzip and meshopt run in workers, and the BVH is built in a worker. What is left on the main thread is the GLTF parse, prepare in 5 ms slices (each slice waits a frame plus a task), the pond scan, the idle plan, and one texture and one compile step per frame. Each BVH job copies position and index arrays on the main thread first.
drivers.where: assets.ts:355-461 (gunzip worker), assets.ts:1130-1164, prepare.ts:505-542 (PREPARE_SLICE_MS 5), bvh-build.ts:104-126 and 159-202
drivers.when: per area load
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same slice budget on every tier; prefetch starts during flight on desktop and at rest on phones (streaming.ts:565).
drivers.costGuess: Un-sliced prepare was 140-580 ms on a 4x-slowed phone (prepare.ts:501-503 comment). At 5 ms per frame that is about 30-115 frames of trickle, so an area can take 0.5-2 s to become ready on a weak phone. This costs latency, not frame time.

drivers.what: Caching. next.config.ts is empty and there is no vercel.json, so /sect/full files get the static-file default (as I understand Vercel's: max-age=0, must-revalidate). manifest, camera, meta and clouds are fetched no-cache on purpose. Every repeat visit sends a conditional request per file before streaming, and the data files cost 2 round trips (manifest first, then the others).
drivers.when: every page load, every file
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier; worst on slow, high-latency phones
drivers.costGuess: About 25-30 files per full sweep, each one at least a round trip even when the answer is 304. Verify with curl -I on a .glb.gz.

drivers.what: JS and the start-up waterfall. The flight is a dynamic ssr:false chunk set, so no GLB request can start until about 545 KB gzip (1.9 MB raw) of JS has downloaded, parsed and mounted. Measured from the Oct 25 build in the main checkout (.next, not rebuilt here): first-load shell about 135 KB gzip, flight chunks about 545 KB gzip (three alone about 190 KB gzip in two chunks, postprocessing about 24 KB, fiber about 52 KB), map-view 9 KB, page-view 59 KB, Retell SDK 128 KB (lazy, on call), pusher 18 KB (lazy). Vercel Analytics and Speed Insights are in the layout.
drivers.when: first visit, before the loading screen can show real progress
drivers.tierBehaviour: Same on every tier; parse cost is highest on weak phones

drivers.what: CSS blur over the canvas. backdrop-filter is on .sect-panel (blur 10px + saturate) and .sect-plate (blur 8px; this wins on elements with both). Used on the area panel (large, bottom of screen), the rail, Map, settings and sound buttons, labels, the hint plates, the talisman tooltip (hover only), lore card. The canvas is not idle at rest: it redraws at 30 fps (20 fps after 20 s of no input), so every visible blur is re-done 20-30 times a second at a stop, and every display frame during flight. Pieces with opacity 0 are not painted. All of it is on at every tier; there is no tier hook in the CSS.
